articles.authors: Sam F. Walmsley, Erik Ringen, Shane Gero, Adrian V. Jaeggi, Hal Whitehead
articles.abstract: Toothed whales offer a 34 My-long natural experiment for the evolution of complex mammalian societies. However, quantitative comparative analyses of social structure in these species are lacking. Here, we draw on existing social network analyses to compare social structure across toothed whales. We consider published measures of two social network traits across all toothed whales: modularity ( Q ), which captures divisions or “cliques” in a social community, and social differentiation ( S ), which estimates how much whales vary in their relationships—whether they associate equally with others or form special bonds with specific individuals. Combining these with a recently published database of life history traits, we applied phylogenetic multilevel models with the objective of exploring the origins of social network structure. We identified 98 measures of modularity and 89 measures of social differentiation from 23 toothed whale species. Social network structure was more similar among closely related species (showing strong phylogenetic signal), despite substantial intraspecific variability. Toothed whales with longer lifespans and larger bodies tended to form more modular social networks, as did those where males were proportionally larger than females. Similar but weaker patterns were found between life history traits and social differentiation. Results from causal coevolutionary models provide preliminary evidence that social structure has been both a leader and follower of changes in life history. Our findings reveal the correlated evolution of social network structure and life history traits in toothed whales, shedding new light on the origins of social relationships.

articles.title: When climate change does not make history
Belonging to a group with shared ideology leads preschool children to resist revising their beliefs despite disconfirming evidence
articles.abstract: Shared beliefs can bring people together but may motivate prioritizing group affiliation over facts supported by evidence. Indeed, affiliation with a group whose membership is tied to shared beliefs (i.e., ideology-based groups) has led adults to endorse and maintain false beliefs. We demonstrate that this resistance to revise beliefs that form the basis of group membership has its origins in childhood. In three studies, 4- to 5-y-old children ( N = 192 ) endorse a claim about a novel causal system and subsequently join a group that shares their endorsement. Children randomly assigned to a focal Belief-contingent condition learn that their membership in the group is based on this claim, framed as a shared belief. We contrast this with conditions where group members hold the same shared belief, but this belief is not a condition for group membership (Experiments 1, 2, and 3), and where group members hold to the same claim framed as a “guess” (Experiment 2). After joining a group, children see evidence that their initial endorsement was incorrect and then have an opportunity to revise based on the new information. Only when group membership was contingent on the shared belief did children hold on to (and act on—Experiment 3) their initial incorrect endorsement. These findings suggest that the affiliative power of ideology has developmental roots; even in our earliest years, affiliative motives override truth-seeking and rationality. Thus, our early-emerging motive to identify with groups may underlie later cases of evidence denial and polarization.

articles.title: Modest loss of sleep increases susceptibility to cybersecurity threats
articles.abstract: Sleep restriction leads to impaired cognitive processing across domains. I examined whether the transition to daylight saving time (DST), typically accompanied by compromised sleep, would lead to an increase in the probability of falling prey to a simulated phishing attack using a fully naturalistic experiment with random assignment and blinding. A predatory email was sent to employees at the University of California, Irvine (N = 11,218) either on the morning of Monday following the transition to DST or one week earlier. The transition led to a ~13% increase in the probability of clicking a suspicious link, without affecting the probability of opening the email or reporting it as spam. These results demonstrate that even modest, mundane, and acute loss of sleep has real-life, potentially hazardous, implications for cognitive function.

articles.title: In-group neural alignment serves as a biomarker of social identity
articles.authors: Yohay Zvi, Nitai Kerem, Eldad Aviv, Yaara Yeshurun
articles.abstract: In this study, we propose a perspective on neural synchronization. Beyond reflecting shared understanding between individuals, we suggest it serves as a biological marker of social homogeneity. We examined fMRI neural responses of 42 participants (21 religious, 21 secular) watching neutral and religion-relevant video narratives. While explicit measures of emotional response, agreement, and engagement showed no significant differences in within-group variance, religious participants—representing a tighter social structure—exhibited significantly higher in-group neural synchrony across all content types and brain networks. Remarkably, synchrony values predicted religious orientation with an accuracy of up to 92%. We conclude that a community’s homogeneous social structure drives pervasive neural alignment, positioning neural synchrony as a potential signature of group cohesion beyond explicit behavioral measures.

articles_hidden.title: IFITM1-mediated restriction of henipavirus entry is associated with ephrinB2 reorganization and confinement in membrane nanodomains
articles_hidden.authors: Yuhang Luo, Jingjing Wang, Jiake Li, Qian Wang, Jacqueline Sung, Vicky Kliemke, Mengyu Zhang, Chen Liang, Qian Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Nipah (NiV) and Hendra (HeV) viruses are prototype henipaviruses (HNV) within the family of Paramyxoviridae . They are highly pathogenic zoonotic paramyxoviruses that cause fatal encephalitis in humans, with case fatality rates of 40 to 70%. These viruses use the receptor-binding protein (G) to engage host receptors ephrinB2 and/or ephrinB3, while the fusion protein (F) drives membrane fusion leading to virus entry and cell–cell fusion. Interferon-inducible transmembrane (IFITM) proteins restrict the infection of many unrelated viruses at virus entry. We show that the knockdown of IFITM1 enhances HNV entry and cell–cell fusion in both human epithelial and endothelial cells, while overexpression of IFITM1 inhibits both. Using single-molecule localization microscopy, we observed that IFITM1 forms nanoclusters on the plasma membrane that are enlarged upon interferon stimulation. IFITM1 clusters spatially co-occur with GM1-enriched, raft-like membrane domains. EphrinB2, a lipid raft resident, organizes into larger and denser clusters when associated with IFITM1, suggesting a preferential partitioning into membrane domains organized and/or influenced by IFITM1. Using single-particle tracking, we further show that lateral diffusion of ephrinB2 on the plasma membrane is confined in the presence of IFITM1. This confinement is not reversed by amphotericin B, nor is IFITM1-mediated NiV restriction. Our data show spatial reorganization and confinement of ephrinB2 within membrane domains that may be organized and/or influenced by IFITM1. These changes may contribute to HNV restriction, potentially by increasing the energy barrier for virus-cell membrane fusion and reducing productive virus-receptor encounters.

articles_hidden.title: Leaf hydraulic and photosynthetic traits mediate forest-scale resource use efficiencies across the continental United States
articles_hidden.authors: Bailu Zhao, Lawren Sack, Hannes Paul T. De Deurwaerder, Camila D. Medeiros, Nidhi Vinod, Marvin Browne, Jeffrey D. Wood, K. C. Cushman, Elena Shevliakova, Sergey Malyshev, Anna Jiselle Ongjoco, Anna Trugman, David A. Orwig, Christina McKeown, Joseph Zailaa, Daniel J. Johnson, Lukas Magee, Sean McMahon, Jess Shue, Karina Schafer, Sean Burns, Peter D. Blanken, Matteo Detto
articles_hidden.abstract: Temperate forests play a critical role in global carbon cycling and other ecosystem services, yet their resilience to climatic stresses remains uncertain. We combined physiology, community composition, flux data, and modeling to test a functional trait-based approach to predict forest ecosystem processes. For eight U.S. forests spanning broad precipitation and temperature gradients, we scaled up key leaf functional traits—maximum carboxylation velocity of Rubisco ( V c , m a x ), maximum leaf hydraulic conductance ( K l , m a x ), and turgor loss point (that is, wilting point, π t l p ) to predict gross primary productivity, light-use efficiency, standard and intrinsic water-use efficiency (WUE and iWUE), and their sensitivities to soil drought. In multiple regressions, ecosystem processes were strongly associated with community-weighted mean (CWM) trait values: enhanced productivity was linked with high V c , m a x ¯ , K l , m a x ¯ and π t l p ¯ , whereas high WUE and iWUE were linked with low K l , m a x ¯ and high π t l p ¯ . The CWM functional traits also influenced the sensitivity of ecosystem processes to soil moisture. A causal role of functional traits in driving ecosystem processes alongside climate was supported by parameterizing the LM4.1 vegetation model with CWM functional traits. This study highlights the important role of functional traits in determining forest responses to climate-driven water stress at a continental scale.

articles_hidden.title: Principles of use of tensile J-curve materials in antagonistic arrangements
articles_hidden.authors: Liuyang Cheng, Wonsik Eom, Qiong Wang, Hyeongkeun Kim, Roberto Pineda Guzman, Jeongmin Kim, Montse Solis, Shreyas Malladi, Samuel Tsai, Mariana E. Kersh, Sameh H. Tawfick
articles_hidden.abstract: Natural ligaments are soft connective tissues that provide high stretchability for dexterous flexibility but switch to high stiffness to protect the musculoskeletal system from excessive deformation. These two functions cannot be independently tuned in conventional engineering materials with linear or hyperelasticity. Biological materials achieve this tailored behavior through a highly nonlinear tensile response characterized by a J-shaped curve, featuring an extended “toe region” of low force up to intermediate strains followed by an inflection, called the “heel region” which marks the onset of nonlinear stiffening. Here, we aim to study the characteristics of J-curves to establish principles for their use in robotic mechanisms. We define and measure the J-curve features responsible for protectiveness and mobility, describe the effective stiffness and the level of nonlinearity as a function of pre-stretch, and elucidate how the J-curve decouples flexibility from damage protection. Experimental measurements reveal the performance advantages of twisted and coiled elastomeric J-curve materials in engineered antagonistic arrangements and highlight their unique design space compared with linear elastic systems. Furthermore, we present a conceptual analysis of exploiting J-curve materials in energy-efficient running as an outlook toward their use in bioinspired robots.

articles_hidden.title: A signal convention in natural chimpanzee communication
articles_hidden.authors: Antoine Valet, Richard Moore, Tatiana Bortolato, Tal Kleinhause G. Gedalyahou, Aude de Witasse-Thézy, Cédric Girard-Buttoz, Roman M. Wittig, Catherine Crockford
articles_hidden.abstract: Human language relies on conventional signals that are arbitrary, stable, and socially transmitted. Whether other animals exhibit meaning-based communicative conventions is virtually unknown. Using a quasi-experimental design, we investigated this in chimpanzee unvoiced calls (UCs), such as acoustic raspberries, known to show usage variation. We collected audio and contextual data in 91 chimpanzees (0 to 55 y), across eight wild and captive groups that differed in the presence or absence of adult role models. Communities with role models emitted UCs in one dominant context, which remained stable over years and from first utterances in development (1 to 2 y old). In contrast, groups without role models displayed highly variable, unstable UC usage across contexts and years. This contextual variation could not be explained by age or by a shared emotional valence, and individuals could use different UC forms within the same context, suggesting a decoupling between the signal form and usage. Together, these findings provide evidence that chimpanzee UCs meet key criteria for a signal convention: arbitrary signal–usage mappings, social transmission, and stability within communities. These findings demonstrate that conventionalized communication is not a uniquely human feature but can also emerge through social learning mechanisms in other animals’ natural communication.

articles_hidden.title: RNA and proteins joined up at the origins of life: Persistence is the point
articles_hidden.authors: Mohamed Swailem, Ken A. Dill
articles_hidden.abstract: What drove nucleic acids (NA) into functional associations with proteins (PR) at the origins of life? We reason from polymer physics and the Central Dogma that the fitness value of cooperating through a division of labor—NA for replication fidelity and PR for functional fitness—is much higher than for either polymer alone. Our model shows a Pareto Front, where NA and PR can bootstrap each other to achieve autocatalytic cooperativity toward biology.

articles_hidden.title: Host and anatomical filters prevent microbiome convergence in avian scavengers
articles_hidden.authors: Antoni Margalida, Antonio Castellano-Hinojosa, Pilar Oliva-Vidal, Sébastien Boutin, José María Martínez, Markus Braun, Hedwig Sauer-Gürth, Karl Schulze-Hagen, Michael Wink
articles_hidden.abstract: How host-associated microbiomes assemble under intense environmental microbial exposure remains a central question in microbial ecology. Vultures represent a unique natural system because these species differ markedly in feeding ecology and carcass use. We characterized bacterial communities across four anatomical niches (facial, buccal, tracheal, and cloacal) in 155 individuals spanning all four European obligate vulture species (subfamily Gypaetinae: Gypaetus barbatus, Neophron percnopterus, and Aegypiinae: Aegypius monachus and Gyps fulvus ) and the facultative scavenger Milvus milvus . Microbiome composition was jointly structured by host species and anatomical niche, with host identity explaining more variation than anatomical compartment and a significant interaction indicating that interspecific differentiation depended on body site. Each niche supported distinct bacterial assemblages and core microbiomes: Cloacal communities were enriched in anaerobic gut-associated taxa, whereas facial and tracheal communities contained more environmental and respiratory-associated bacteria. Host-specific taxonomic signatures persisted within anatomical niches despite recurrent exposure to the same carrion-associated microbial pool. Age further influenced community composition, whereas sex had little detectable effect. The facultative scavenger showed the same broad anatomical compartmentalization observed in obligate scavengers, although taxonomic signatures differed among species. Thus, sustained exposure to a shared, microbially rich resource was insufficient to produce a common scavenger microbiome. Instead, microbiome assembly reflected hierarchical filtering by host identity, anatomical environment, and ontogeny. These findings distinguish microbial exposure from microbial persistence, establishing avian scavengers as a natural model for understanding how host-associated communities remain differentiated, despite recurrent exposure to shared environmental microbial reservoirs across ecological and anatomical scales in vertebrate hosts.

articles_hidden.title: Physiologic and pharmacologic role of the glucocorticoid receptor in germinal center B cells and plasmacytic differentiation
articles_hidden.authors: Clarissa Corinaldesi, Antony B. Holmes, Chuanjiang Yu, Zeinab Amini-Farsani, Qiong Shen, Tongwei Mo, Eli Grunstein, Govind Bhagat, Katia Basso, Riccardo Dalla-Favera, Laura Pasqualucci
articles_hidden.abstract: In diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), a malignancy derived from germinal center (GC) B cells, somatic hypermutation aberrantly targets glucocorticoid receptor (GR) binding sequences in the super-enhancer (SE) of multiple oncogenes. These events abrogate GR binding and deregulate the expression of the SE-linked gene, suggesting an important role of GR in normal and transformed GC B cells. Using a GC-specific Nr3c1 knockout mouse model and multi-omics analyses in murine and human GC B cells, here we show that, under physiological conditions, GR constitutively localizes to the nucleus, where it transcriptionally modulates signaling pathways implicated in GC homeostasis and plasmablast differentiation in part by antagonizing the repressive function of BCL6 on the plasma cell master regulators IRF4 and PRDM1. While loss of baseline GR activity led to mild GC hyperplasia and impaired plasmacytic differentiation, pharmacologic doses of glucocorticoids, a key component of DLBCL chemo-immunotherapy, were preferentially toxic to GC in a GC B cell–autonomous manner. These findings uncover a physiological role for GR in the GC reaction as well as in promoting plasmablast/plasma cell formation and provide insights into the specific activity of glucocorticoids in the treatment of DLBCL.

articles_hidden.title: Evolutionary dynamics of collective behavior across the tree of ray-finned fishes
articles_hidden.authors: Jay Love, Amlan Nayak, Abigail G. Grassick, Ling-Wei Kong, Ella G. Henry, Michael A. Gil, Ashkaan K. Fahimipour, Matt Pennell, Andrew M. Hein
articles_hidden.abstract: Trait evolution and lineage diversification are thought to be driven by selection on the phenotypes of individuals. However, many important phenotypes are only manifested when individuals interact. Collective behavior is one such phenotype. During collective behavior, interactions among individuals lead to emergent group-level phenotypes that can govern individual fitness. Yet, whether collective behaviors exhibit similar patterns of trait evolution to individual traits and whether these group phenotypes have influenced macroevolutionary diversification is unknown. In ray-finned fishes, the most species-rich of all vertebrate classes, many species exhibit striking displays of collective behavior in the form of collective movement. Here, we use state-of-the-art machine learning methods for text and image analysis to quantify collective movement phenotypes for 2,839 Actinopterygian fishes, comprising nearly 10% of all extant species. We find that collective movement is highly evolutionarily stable in some clades and extremely labile in others, exhibiting over 300 evolutionary transitions. Consistent with theoretical predictions, collective movement is associated with more patchy diets and higher predation pressure. Finally, we find that the evolution of collective movement coincides with an increase in net macroevolutionary diversification rate. Our analyses reveal that collective behavior is deeply intertwined with ecological and evolutionary dynamics across a vast phylogenetic scale, unlocking questions about the evolution of collective phenotypes and their role in shaping the diversity of life on Earth.

articles_hidden.title: Signaling mechanism of the transmembrane energy receptor Aer
articles_hidden.authors: Flory A. Olsthoorn, Alise R. Muok, Zachary A. Maschmann, Yajie Xu, Siddarth Chandrasekaran, Robert Dunleavy, Brian R. Crane
articles_hidden.abstract: The Escherichia coli aerotaxis receptor Aer is a bacterial chemoreceptor that senses intracellular redox changes via an N-terminal PAS domain bound to a flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) cofactor. Distinct from canonical methyl-accepting chemotaxis proteins (MCPs) such as Tar/Tsr, Aer lacks a periplasmic ligand-binding domain and adaptive methylation, transmitting conformational signals laterally from the PAS domain to the HAMP domain and the methylation helix-like cap (MHL-cap) of the kinase control domain (KCD). To elucidate the Aer signaling mechanism, we determined cryoelectron microscopy structures of full-length Aer in oxidized flavin quinone (kinase-on) and reduced semiquinone (kinase-off) states. Structural comparison reveals redox-linked rearrangements of the FAD-binding pocket, reorientation of PAS–HAMP interactions, and strikingly altered MHL-cap stability. PAS–MHL-cap interactions in the oxidized state compress the receptor and stabilize the proximal KCD helices, whereas reduction disrupts these contacts, increasing KCD flexibility. To probe distal effects on KCD architecture, we performed nanodisc reconstitution and pulse dipolar ESR spectroscopy on spin-labeled positions along the four-helix bundle. Distance distributions indicate redox-dependent changes in helix separation, particularly at the C-terminal MHL2 region, consistent with PAS-driven loosening of KCD packing in kinase-off states. These data support a model in which FAD redox chemistry reorganizes flavin pocket residues that in turn subtly alter PAS conformation to influence PAS–HAMP and PAS–MHL-cap packing and hence KCD conformational stability. The findings reveal an Aer-specific signaling axis distinct from periplasmic-ligand binding MCPs that has adapted MCP architecture for lateral PAS input and cytoplasmic redox sensing.

articles_hidden.title: Structural basis of hypervariable region 1 dynamics on HCV envelope glycoproteins in immune evasion
articles_hidden.authors: Shr-Hau Hung, Yukiye Koide, Fang Chen, Yi-Zong Lee, Lynn A. Ueno, Erick Giang, Ian A. Wilson, Jiang Zhu, Robyn L. Stanfield, Mansun Law
articles_hidden.abstract: The hypervariable region 1 (HVR1) of the hepatitis C virus E1E2 glycoprotein plays a crucial role in immune evasion through rapid mutation and shielding of conserved neutralizing epitopes. Despite its important role, the structural properties of HVR1 remain poorly understood, particularly how its conformation influences shielding mechanisms and receptor recognition. To date in all published E1E2 or E2 structures, the C-terminal part of HVR1 (394 to 411) remains unresolved. Using neutralizing antibody (nAb) RM1-38, which targets C-terminal HVR1 (residues 399 to 409), we investigated the folding, positioning, flexibility, and shielding function of the RM1-38 epitope, or antigenic site 399 (AS399), on HVR1 by X-ray crystallography and negative-stain electron microscopy (nsEM). The crystal structure of RM1-38 Fab with the HVR1 AS399 peptide, combined with mutagenesis analysis, delineated the molecular basis of its strain-specific recognition and neutralization. nsEM and competition enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay revealed that HVR1 exhibits pronounced conformational flexibility even in the presence of other nAbs bound to E1E2. Virus neutralization assays using a combination of RM1-38 and broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) demonstrated antagonistic effects of RM1-38 with the bnAbs. Furthermore, RM1-38 reduced E1E2 binding to cells expressing the scavenger receptor SR-BI, an HVR1-dependent receptor, but did not affect binding to CD81 tetraspanin. Together, these findings support a model in which HVR1 functions as a dynamic shield, where its conformational plasticity contributes to both receptor engagement and evasion of humoral immunity in persistent infection.

articles_hidden.title: Programmable multistable structures via bioinspired, mechanically guided 4D printing
articles_hidden.authors: Yan Zhao, Hanlin Zhu, Yifeng He, Yilong Zhang, Xin Ye, Rui Lv, Yuanyuan Tian, Zhixun Wang, Jinwu Xiang, Shiwei Zhao, Kun Zhou, Chao Jiang
articles_hidden.abstract: Multistable structures, characterized by rapid shape morphing, instantaneous force amplification, and zero standby power, are pivotal for soft robotics and energy harvesting. However, achieving multistability while systematically controlling the accessible deformation modes remains a significant challenge. Here, we report a bioinspired, mechanically guided 4D printing approach to design and fabricate programmable multistable structures, including octastable and various bistable units, mimicking the growth-induced morphing of plant leaves and fruits. The stability landscapes of these units can be tuned by varying dimensionless geometric parameters and validated through buckling analysis. By integrating multiple octastable units, we demonstrate a compact, 10-cm-scale strip and a shape-morphing metasurface with configuration spaces of over one billion and four sextillion stable states. Furthermore, by modulating the dimensionless geometric parameters of multiunit structures, we identify a transition from bending to folding, enabling the creation of bistable hinges. As proof-of-concept demonstrations, we developed devices for directional droplet routing and mixing, reconfigurable electrical switching, conforming grasping of irregular objects, and programmable mechanical display. This work establishes a versatile framework for the design and fabrication of next-generation reconfigurable morphing systems and programmable flexible devices.

articles_hidden.title: Linear scaling reveals low-dimensional structure in observable microbial dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Zhengqing Zhou, Xiaoli Chen, Yasa Baig, Wendy Kehan Wang, Emrah Şimşek, Grayson S. Hamrick, Zachary A. Holmes, Zhenjiao Du, David K. Karig, Lingchong You
articles_hidden.abstract: Microbial communities often exhibit apparently complex dynamics driven by myriad interactions among community members and with their environments. Yet, practical modeling and control are often based on a limited number of observables, raising fundamental questions: are these observed dynamics low-dimensional? If so, how does the low dimensionality enable predictions with limited information? Here, we report an emergent simplicity that the temporal dynamics of observable microbial populations can be captured by low-dimensional representations. Using variational autoencoders, we define a critical latent dimension ( E c ) that operationally quantifies the smallest latent dimension required for high-fidelity reconstruction of observable microbial dynamics under a specified criterion. Despite the complexity of unobserved background dynamics, we find E c to be drastically lower than the community’s apparent degrees of freedom. E c scales linearly with the number of observables, providing an empirical principle for determining representation complexity. This principle holds across simulations of pairwise interacting communities, consumer–resource dynamics, spatially distributed microbial patches, and plasmid transfer, experiments with engineered and environment-derived communities, and human microbiomes. Our findings establish a scaling law for microbial community dynamics and demonstrate that low-dimensional representations of observable dynamics retain information useful for selected prediction tasks without direct measurement of the complete community.

articles_hidden.title: Phase transition in a dryland shrub–grass ecosystem: Emergence through local trade-offs
articles_hidden.authors: Jingyao Sun, Kailiang Yu, Xinrong Li, Max Rietkerk, Paolo D’Odorico, Ning Chen, Yanli Wang, Libin Zhang, Guirui Yu
articles_hidden.abstract: Ecosystems are complex adaptive systems in which local interactions among individuals shape macroscopic phenomena such as pattern formation, multistability, and critical transitions. However, how such bottom-up interactions govern emergent behaviors and system-level complexity remains a central challenge in ecology. Phase transition theory, a classic paradigm in physics, links local interaction rules to emergent changes in macroscopic system states, offering a formal language for understanding cross-scale dynamics. Here we unite this theory with empirical evidence from dryland shrub–grass ecosystems and show that these systems exhibit three hallmarks of phase transitions. First, abrupt shifts separate different phases of deserts, shrublands, and grasslands. Second, shrublands and grasslands self-organize into Turing-like phase patterns, contrasting with homogeneous deserts. Third, special phenomena emerge near-transition threshold, including patch enlargement and abrupt decline at desert–vegetation interface, and fairy circles within the shrub–grass transition zone. Using a cellular automaton model built on a fundamental trade-off between extensive and intensive resource foraging strategies (EI trade-off), we show how kernels encoding local trade-offs integrate these seemingly disparate phenomena within a unified phase transition framework. Moreover, this EI trade-off was empirically validated through analyses of plant functional traits and spatial patterns of plant patches. These findings illustrate that dryland ecosystem dynamics reflect universal self-organization principles. Our work establishes phase-transition theory as a powerful framework for understanding, predicting, and managing complexity in dryland ecosystems, which advances the integration of complexity science with ecology, offering a pathway toward bottom-up ecosystem understanding.

articles_hidden.title: Multi-omics characterization of white matter free water reveals genetic and vascular determinants of neurological disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Chang Cheng, Yuqin He, Xi Cao, Shizhen Xiang, Yuanyuan Fang, Mengying Wang, Zhonghe Shao, Yao Yao, Hao Huang, Shabei Xu, Xiang Luo, Xiaopeng Zong, Wei Wang, Xingjie Hao, Minghuan Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: White matter free water (FW-WM), quantified using diffusion MRI, reflects extracellular water content and microstructural alterations within water matter, but its genetic architecture and clinical relevance remain largely uncharted. We conducted a multi-omics study integrating 42,039 individuals from the UK Biobank and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohorts to characterize tract-specific FW-WM across genetic, phenotypic, and proteomic dimensions. Genome-wide association analyses identified 27 independent loci and prioritized 88 genes, which were enriched in the genomic functional elements of vascular endothelial cells, pericytes, and astrocytes. Notably, 20 loci (74%) were novel compared to conventional white matter metrics. Both genetic predisposition to higher FW-WM and imaging-derived FW-WM were associated with a spectrum of neurological disorders. Specifically, imaging-derived FW-WM showed strong associations with stroke (OR = 3.14) and dementia (OR = 4.15), while higher baseline FW-WM predicted progression from MCI to AD (HR = 2.58). Bidirectional Mendelian randomization analyses further supported genetically predicted associations between hypertension and FW-WM, which were together associated with increased risks of stroke and cognitive impairment. Integrative proteomic analyses further nominated PEAR1 and ANGL3 as candidate proteins potentially linking hypertension-related vascular processes to FW-WM variation. Together, these findings provide a multi-omics characterization of FW-WM that connects genetic susceptibility, vascular factors, and neurological outcomes, supporting FW-WM as a tract-specific imaging phenotype with potential utility for neurological risk stratification.

articles_hidden.title: A replaceable soma enables negative senescence in harvester ants
articles_hidden.authors: Blaine J. Cole, Diane C. Wiernasz
articles_hidden.abstract: Most vertebrates and insects undergo senescence: as they age, their rate of mortality increases while reproduction declines. We present data from a 34-y study on 3,285 colonies of known age in the western harvester ant, Pogonomyrmex occidentalis, that show the reverse pattern, negative senescence, in which mortality decreases and reproduction increases with age. Theoretical models have identified indeterminate growth and a lack of reproductive cost to growth as the key traits favoring the evolution of negative senescence. Ant colonies continue to grow throughout their lifetime, leading to older colonies being larger on average. We found no evidence of a tradeoff between colony growth and reproduction: growth and reproduction were positively correlated, a synergism that may favor continued investment in growth. Harvester ants occupy a temporally variable environment that shapes investment in reproduction. At the population level, greater reproduction in 1 y does not lead to higher numbers of new colonies in the following year. Environmental unpredictability decouples reproduction from recruitment and selects for an extended reproductive lifespan, a trait that parallels changes in aging. We discuss the features that harvester ant colonies share with other organisms to identify functionally homologous mechanisms for avoiding senescence, as well as those traits that are specific to highly eusocial species.

articles_hidden.title: Host infection selects for sRNA variants that drive bacterial social cheating
articles_hidden.authors: Quentin Dubois, Typhaine Brual, Marcel Sprenger, Véronique Utzinger, Romain Mercier, Jérémy Cigna, Agnès Rodrigue, Kai Papenfort, Laetitia Attaiech, Erwan Gueguen
articles_hidden.abstract: Single-nucleotide mutations in regulatory small RNAs (sRNAs) represent a largely unexplored route to social cheating during bacterial infection. Here we show that arcZ , encoding a conserved Hfq-dependent sRNA in the plant pathogen Dickeya solani , undergoes recurrent single-nucleotide mutations during potato tuber infection. Five distinct arcZ alleles define a graded series of ArcZ functional impairment in which antifungal and protease activities are progressively reduced while virulence is compromised only in a subset of alleles. All five variants gain a fitness advantage exclusively during coinfection with wild-type arcZ 1 cells. This advantage is strongest when variants are rare and declines as cheater frequency increases, ultimately correlating with reduced total bacterial productivity, the canonical signature of social cheating and a tragedy of the commons. No fitness benefit is detected in vitro . Transcriptomic profiling of five arcZ variants identifies a conserved core of 186 downregulated genes enriched in secreted and diffusible functions. Systematic genetic dissection, supported by quantitative proteomics, establishes BudAB-dependent limitation of tissue acidification as the dominant cooperative public good exploited during infection. Wild-type arcZ 1 cells divert pyruvate flux toward acetoin via the BudAB pathway, maintaining a less acidic tissue environment that sustains disease progression; arcZ variants, which show reduced expression of this pathway, benefit from the less acidic environment maintained by wild-type cells without contributing to it. These results establish pleiotropic regulatory sRNAs as a previously unrecognized class of mutational targets for the emergence of social cheaters during host infection.

articles_hidden.title: Polarized twin walls in a halide perovskite
articles_hidden.authors: Weilun Li, Qimu Yuan, Michael B. Johnston, Joanne Etheridge
articles_hidden.abstract: Halide perovskites have emerged as promising materials for next-generation photovoltaics, laser sources, and X-ray detectors. There is intense debate as to whether some photoactive halide perovskites exhibit ferroelectric behavior and whether it might be possible to utilize the bulk photovoltaic effect to enhance the performance of halide perovskite solar cells. Here, using low-dose scanning transmission electron microscopy, we identify ferroelastic twin walls in vapor-deposited CsPbI 3 thin films, parallel to {110} and {112}. Remarkably, despite CsPbI 3 being centrosymmetric and nonpolar, we observe directly that Pb atoms shift at {110} twin walls driving a local ferroelectric-like polarization. These polar twin walls form an intrinsic array of nanoscale interfaces, spaced ~30 to 50 nm apart, embedded within the nonpolar perovskite lattice. In contrast, {112} twin walls do not show a polar displacement of Pb but strongly suppress octahedral tilt and off-center Cs atom displacements, revealing a different untapped structural degree of freedom. These findings reveal previously hidden nanoscale polarization in halide perovskite semiconductors, opening opportunities for enhanced conductivity and photovoltaic behavior through domain wall engineering.

articles_hidden.title: Sub-ice thermal gradients strongly influence winter depth use of an iconic cold-water fish
articles_hidden.authors: Lidi Shi, Mathew G. Wells, Mark S. Ridgway, Erin S. Dunlop, Bailey C. McMeans, Aaron T. Fisk, Paul J. Blanchfield, Steven J. Cooke, Michael D. Rennie, Joelle D. Young, Trevor A. Middel, Justin Trumpickas, Lee E. Hrenchuk, Benjamin L. Hlina, Matthew M. Guzzo
articles_hidden.abstract: In a thermally stratified lake, freshwater fish select habitats that align with their thermal preferences. While most studies of dimictic lakes have focused on habitat selection during summer stratification, less attention has been given to winter when inverse thermal stratification occurs with water temperatures between 0 to 4 °C. Our results show that winter thermal stratifications vary considerably among lakes. Much of the variation in winter depth use by the cold-water predator, Lake Trout ( Salvelinus namaycush ), can be explained by the depth of the 2 °C isotherm. Selection ratios further support preferential use of this thermal boundary after accounting for habitat availability. Larger, shallower, and windier lakes tend to exhibit colder mean temperatures near 0 °C and deeper isotherms, typically within the 1 to 2 °C range. In contrast, deeper or more sheltered lakes maintained warmer temperatures close to 4 °C and a shallower 2 °C isotherm. Using multiyear acoustic telemetry of Lake Trout from 11 different lakes, we found that in warmer lakes with depth-averaged temperatures above 2 °C, Lake Trout used thermal habitat averaging 2.6 ± 0.6 °C, which occurred in relatively shallow depths (0.1 to 11.3 m). In contrast, in the one large, shallow lake studied, where maximum water temperatures were below 2 °C, Lake Trout occupied the deepest waters during winter (16.8 to 26.4 m) and experienced average temperatures of 1.5 ± 0.4 °C. Applying our model to 877,927 Canadian and Alaskan lakes predicted a roughly even split between warm and cold winter conditions; however, 73% of the 66,500 known Lake Trout lakes exhibited warmer winter conditions, where Lake Trout would occupy the upper water column during winter.

articles_hidden.title: Optimal scenario design for climate emulation
articles_hidden.authors: Christopher B. Womack, Shahine Bouabid, Andrei Sokolov, Popat Salunke, Glenn Flierl, Sebastian D. Eastham, Noelle E. Selin
articles_hidden.abstract: As deep learning for physical systems continues to grow in popularity, efforts to improve generalizability have primarily focused on designing architectures that embed physical constraints. However, for machine-learning surrogate climate models (emulators), we show that the low structural diversity in existing scenarios commonly used to generate training data places a ceiling on predictive skill. Here, we examine whether training datasets themselves can be optimized to improve generalization. We introduce a method to create datasets that produce emulators capable of generalizing to new, structurally different scenarios absent from the training data. We use a differentiable simple climate model (SCM) to calculate the sensitivity of emulator loss to perturbations in the training data, iteratively updating the training data to maximize emulator skill. For an SCM, an emulator trained on one scenario optimized in this fashion outperforms an emulator trained on six standard Scenario Model Intercomparison Project (ScenarioMIP) pathways. We achieve this higher predictive skill despite training on a smaller dataset, finding that our emulator successfully isolates distinct physical behaviors of different climate forcing agents (e.g., greenhouse gases vs. aerosols) without single-forcing runs. We then demonstrate that scenarios optimized using an SCM, when used to drive an intermediate-complexity climate model, produce a training dataset that yields a more skillful emulator than training on ScenarioMIP outputs. Our results suggest that, in the compute-constrained environment of running full-scale climate models, generating a small number of dynamically rich scenarios provides greater marginal value for emulation and characterizing system responses than expanding the suite of traditional emissions pathways.

articles_hidden.title: Phosphatases regulating ERK activation and ERK-dependent cell migration
articles_hidden.authors: Yue Li, Huanle Li, Tianfeng Lu, Qingcui Li, Wenrui Dou, Xiaoyi Zhu, Ming Zhong, Qiang Zhao, Junhui Guo, Thomas B. Kornberg, Honggang Wu, Xiaokun Shu, Hai Huang
articles_hidden.abstract: Extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs) have essential roles in development and are implicated in numerous diseases. ERKs are activated by phosphorylation and are regulated by dephosphorylation. To study the ERK phosphatases, we adapted a method to monitor ERK activity in live, unfixed preparations that accommodates the highly dynamic temporal and spatial features of ERK activation. We evaluated 140 human phosphatases using an in vivo reporter (ERK-SPARK) for high-throughput screening in human cells, and we used an in vivo Drosophila model for functional validation of their phosphatase homologs. We found that EYA family phosphatases are critical regulators of ERK signaling both in Drosophila and in mammalian cells and found that inhibition of human EYA4, a homolog of Drosophila Eyes Absent phosphatase, enhances migration of ERK-responsive tumor cells. These findings have important implications for the development of therapeutics.

articles_hidden.title: Active and passive crowding pathways drive topological and mechanical divergence in myoblasts
articles_hidden.authors: Yucheng Huo, Hongmei Xu, Kexin Guo, Yukai Zhao, Bryant Doss, Quan Zhou, Yueying Wang, Xiaofei Ju, Endao Han, Changjin Huang, K. Jimmy Hsia
articles_hidden.abstract: Cell crowding is closely associated with many physiological processes, yet our understanding of crowded tissue organization has been developed largely in polygonal epithelia, leaving intrinsically anisotropic cell collectives comparatively poorly understood. Using C2C12 myoblasts, we investigate this problem by decoupling the final crowded state from the pathway taken to reach it, comparing active crowding, arising from cell proliferation during incubation, with passive crowding, imposed directly through high-density seeding. Unlike polygonal epithelia, crowded myoblast monolayers do not undergo epithelial-like kinetic arrest: cell motion is strongly suppressed, yet local rearrangements persist and packing remains structurally irregular. However, the two crowding pathways generate distinct collective states, differing in nematic order and junctional coupling. By contrasting these states, we reveal a close interplay among cell geometry, intercellular coupling, tissue-scale nematic order, and force transmission. This mechanical coordination ultimately shapes physiological function, preserving sensitivity to topographical cues and promoting efficient, spatially organized myogenic fusion. These findings broaden the physical framework of collective organization in active matter and establish key mechanical principles for in vitro tissue engineering.

articles_hidden.title: Millennial-scale variability in Greenland dust provenance during Dansgaard–Oeschger events of the last glacial period
articles_hidden.authors: Seokhyun Ro, Changhee Han, Yeongcheol Han, Soon Do Hur, Chul-Un Ro, Jørgen Peder Steffensen, Anders Svensson, Hubertus Fischer, Andrea Burke, Khanghyun Lee, Ahhyung Lee, Sungmin Hong
articles_hidden.abstract: Greenland ice-core records show an approximately 15-fold increase in dust concentration during cold stadial periods compared to warmer interstadial periods in the last glacial period (LGP). While multiple regions including East Asian deserts and the Sahara have been suggested as potential source areas (PSAs) for Greenland dust, millennial-scale variability of their relative contributions associated with Dansgaard–Oeschger climatic fluctuations during the LGP remains poorly constrained. To address this, we investigate high-resolution (~800 y) Pb and Sr isotopic, mineralogical, and geochemical records from the North Greenland Eemian Ice Drilling ice-core samples covering the entire LGP. We found that the Pb and Sr isotopic compositions, kaolinite-to-chlorite ratios, and chemical index of alteration values were higher during stadials than during interstadials. Comparison with PSAs suggests that East Asian deserts remained the dominant contributors to Greenland dust throughout the LGP, but contributions from the Sahara increased during stadial intervals. This shift likely reflects climate-driven changes in atmospheric circulation patterns responsible for transporting dust to Greenland. Our findings provide insights into the relationship between dust cycle dynamics and abrupt climate changes on millennial timescales during the LGP.
