BiSMR couples an E 2 -loaded PLTG [poly( l -lactide)- co -trimethylene carbonate- co -glycolic acid] backbone with a PDA-EGCG@HAMA coating, enabling rapid EGCG release followed by sustained E 2 delivery. In vitro, BiSMR promoted cell proliferation, migration, angiogenesis, and M2 polarization while suppressing myofibroblast transition. In rat IUA models, BiSMR restored endometrial structure and vascularization, reduced fibrosis, and improved implantation and live birth rates. Proteomics revealed down-regulation of fibrosis- and inflammation-related effectors and restoration of protein biosynthesis and regenerative pathways. BiSMR offers a promising strategy for IUA therapy and fertility restoration.

articles_hidden.title: Age reshapes selection on melanoma driver mutations
articles_hidden.authors: Yihan Liu, Jeffrey D. Mandell, Moein Rajaei, Douglas Brash, Jorge Alfaro-Murillo, Jeffrey P. Townsend
articles_hidden.abstract: Aging is a major risk factor for melanoma. However, it is unclear whether aging fuels tumor evolution by altering mutation rates, changing the microenvironmentally induced selection on drivers, or both. We analyzed 5472 melanomas, estimating how selection on individual variants changes with patient age while accounting for differing neutral mutation rates. Neutral mutation rates increased only modestly with age; ultraviolet damage remained predominant, but endogenous processes increasingly contributed to older tumors. In contrast, selection on major drivers was strongly age dependent: The advantage of BRAF V600E declined precipitously with age, whereas NRAS Q61 mutations gained advantage. TERT promoter mutations became more frequent, yet less advantageous. Aging therefore reshapes melanoma evolution primarily by altering selection, motivating age-conscious evaluation of clinical biomarkers and therapies.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting the additionality and durability of carbon uptake in large-scale ocean iron fertilization
articles_hidden.authors: Kyung-Min Noh, Xiao Liu, Charles Stock, Dennis J. McGillicuddy, John Dunne
articles_hidden.abstract: Climate stabilization pathways limiting global warming to 1.5° to 2°C require rapid emission reductions alongside additional carbon dioxide removal (CDR) of ∼2 to 3 PgC year −1 . Our simulations show that sustained century-scale ocean iron fertilization (OIF) in the southern sector of the Southern Ocean (SSO) provides a contribution of ∼30 PgC, equivalent to ∼0.3 PgC year −1 . This uptake nearly matches the additional carbon uptake from global fertilization. In other iron-limited regions, fertilization-induced uptake is largely offset (70 to 100%) by anomalous outgassing in nonfertilized regions. After terminating OIF following 30 years of fertilization, the ocean retains ∼50% of the additional carbon in the SSO, whereas retention is negligible elsewhere. These results identify the SSO as the most favorable region for durable carbon removal through large-scale OIF, particularly in terms of additionality and durability, although its carbon uptake is smaller than earlier estimates. OIF-induced CDR is constrained by local and remote nutrient depletion, carbon reentrainment, incomplete macronutrient drawdown, and reduced phytoplankton carbon-to-phosphorus ratios. Incomplete macronutrient drawdown reflects the uptake controls by light, top-down controls, and rates of macronutrient resupply. Further insight into OIF potential will be enabled by standardized multimodel comparisons and targeted analysis of nutrient drawdown controls.

articles_hidden.title: Combating drug-resistant Aeromonas veronii : Multiomics revealed the antibacterial mechanism of resveratrol
articles_hidden.authors: Ping Ouyang, Minmin Wang, Xiaonan Li, Fen Chen, Bowen Liu, Kaiyi Yin, Nan Zhang, Jiyang Xiao, Chenhui Zhang, Yi Geng, Xiaoli Huang, Defang Chen
articles_hidden.abstract: Aeromonas , widely distributed in aquatic ecosystems, is a prevalent fish pathogen and can cause human infections via contaminated aquatic products, polluted water contact, or tainted food consumption. Escalating antibiotic resistance in Aeromonas strains highlights an urgent need for alternative natural antimicrobial agents. This study investigated resveratrol’s antibacterial mechanisms against Aeromonas veronii and evaluated its protective efficacy in hybrid sturgeon. Resveratrol exhibited strong activity [minimum inhibitory concentration: 128 microgram per milliliter (μg/ml), minimum bactericidal concentration: 256 μg/ml], disrupting cell wall/membrane integrity, inducing reactive oxygen species accumulation, inhibiting adenosine 5′-triphosphate synthesis, and down-regulating key metabolic pathways via transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses. In the sturgeon infection model, resveratrol-nanoemulsion notably improved survival, reduced tissue bacterial loads, mitigated oxidative stress and inflammation, and restored intestinal barrier function. These findings confirm resveratrol as a promising antibiotic alternative against A. veronii , with nanoemulsion formulation enhancing its therapeutic efficacy.

articles_hidden.title: Adaptive dual-programming magnetic soft robot with lifelike behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Yanchen Ye, Can Xu, Sen Wang, Weijia Li, RongYe Wu, Hao Wu, Neng Xia, TianYe Yang, Shuang Song, Li Zhang, Yue Dong, Bing Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Magnetic soft robots with embodied intelligence of multimodal motions, environmental perception, and functional decoupling depend on ingenious material arrangement and programmable morphing information introduction. While some efforts have been made, achieving lifelike behaviors for soft robots in system-level strategy remains a notable challenge. Here, we present dual-programming hydrogel-based soft robots (DHSRs) that couple magnetic and anisotropic programming through the spatial arrangement of patterned magnetic skeletons into responsive and structural hydrogel bodies. These DHSRs exhibit programmable exquisite and multicurved structures in three-dimensional (3D) space, environment-adaptive deformation behaviors proved by switching from random jumping on land to regular swimming in water of a fish-like soft robot, and further locomotion-function decoupling capabilities of region-selective cargo delivery in an integrated “locomotion-perception-action” workflow. Our strategy in biomedical potential is exemplified by a ring-like pH-responsive DHSR for gastric ulcer therapy, which integrates multimodal locomotion (rolling, tumbling, and rotating), adaptive matching, and microneedle-mediated penetration. By collaborating with a capsule endoscopy system, we explore the possibility of a wireless and painless diagnostic-therapeutic platform in a pig model. This strategy endows the robot with perception and multitask execution capabilities, highlighting a promising route for the intelligent evolution of soft robots across diverse application domains.

articles_hidden.title: Piezoelectrically actuated magnetic dipole twisting resonators enable miniaturized low-frequency antennas
articles_hidden.authors: Jianglei Chang, Bohan Li, Xiangyu Gao, Kexin Song, Yaojin Wang, Jie Jiao, Davresh Hasanyan, Shujun Zhang, Fei Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Miniaturized low-frequency antennas are essential for underwater, underground, and biomedical communications, yet their performance is constrained by the fundamental size-efficiency trade-off, a long-standing physical bottleneck. Here, we introduce a radiation mechanism that circumvents this constraint by replacing the time-varying currents in conventional antennas with the mechanical twisting oscillation of a magnetic dipole. Using piezoelectrically actuated, biomimetic twisting resonators with ultrahigh mechanical quality factors, we demonstrate that low-frequency antennas operating at 15.4 and 668 hertz can be miniaturized to centimeter- and millimeter-scale, respectively, with radiation efficiencies exceeding those of size-matched loop antennas by factors of 49,000 and 5000, respectively. This electromechanical-magnetic transduction enables underwater cross-medium communication over 115 meters with only milliwatt-level power consumption, using 99.9% less power than loop antennas. It also supports implantable wireless devices that achieve a fourfold increase in communication range at identical power consumption, opening a route to long-range, low-power wireless systems capable of operating in some of the most demanding environments.

articles_hidden.title: Controllable fabrication of visible-spectrum 3D photonic crystals
articles_hidden.authors: Huace Hu, Daqian Li, Hui Gao, Fayu Chen, Mingduo Zhang, Zongjing Li, Aofei Mao, Wei Xiong
articles_hidden.abstract: The fabrication of visible-spectrum three-dimensional (3D) photonic crystals (PhCs) remains highly challenging, because existing manufacturing techniques cannot simultaneously achieve high processing precision and sufficient geometric freedom. Here, we propose a suspended pyrolysis-assisted two-photon polymerization (SP-TPP) printing strategy, achieving the controllable fabrication of visible-spectrum 3D PhCs. The resulting 3D diamond PhCs exhibit a remarkable lattice-period standard deviation of only 5.75 nm, approximately 1/45 of that achieved without suspended pyrolysis. Microscopic reflection spectra confirm these PhCs possess uniform optical responses across all spatial positions. By tuning the lattice period and structural duty cycle, the PhCs operating at diverse wavelengths are systematically realized. Moreover, through the demonstration of PhC prototype structures and in situ arrayed fabrication, the SP-TPP printing strategy paves the way for applications in photonic microcavities, 3D optical waveguides, optical splitters, and integrated micro-optical systems.

articles_hidden.title: The transcription factors OsIDD and OsSHR jointly regulate ground tissue patterning and differentiation in rice roots
articles_hidden.authors: Liyun Peng, Zhufeng Chen, Ziheng Li, Shuling Cao, Jinge Liu, Ruiting Liu, Jinyu Yu, Baolei Zhang, Xiaoyu Liang, Bocheng Gao, Xingxiang Chen, Jixing Xia
articles_hidden.abstract: Rice roots have a distinctive ground tissue architecture with multiple cortical layers and a single endodermal layer concentrically surrounding the stele. This architecture promotes aerenchyma formation and adaptability to waterlogged environments, but the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely unexplored. Here, we identified the INDETERMINATE DOMAIN (IDD) and SHORTROOT (SHR) families as key regulators of ground tissue development in rice. OsIDD2/3/6/8 govern cortical radial symmetry by coordinating cortical organization and auxin distribution independently of OsSHR1/2/3/4/5. Quadruple knockout of OsIDD2/3/6/8 caused cortical asymmetry without affecting apoplastic barrier integrity or mineral uptake but reduced shoot-directed ion transport. OsIDD8 also controls the number of cortical cell layers and endodermal cells, whereas OsSHR1/2/3/4/5 redundantly promote periclinal divisions of the cortical cells, which require OsIDD8 activity. Moreover, OsIDD and OsSHR members coordinate endodermal differentiation by regulating localization of Casparian strip membrane domain protein OsCASP1 and lignin/suberin deposition. These findings establish a genetic framework underlying the spatial organization and functional differentiation of ground tissue in rice roots.

articles_hidden.title: Multimodal switches exploiting electromechanical snap-through for versatile robotic information processing
articles_hidden.authors: Shengjun Fan, Jianglong Guo, Fei Jia, Jian Sun, Yanju Liu, Metin Sitti
articles_hidden.abstract: It is highly desirable to design and engineer lightweight, low-power-consumption, and rapid physical intelligence (PI) structures that couple with multiple robotic functions. Here, we present a multimodal electromechanical switch (mEMS), consisting of a stretchable droplet-amplified electrostatic zipping structure, a convex bump, and a pair of electrical contacts, that can be used to achieve the widely used mechanical momentary, mechanical latching, and electrically actuated switching modes by simply tuning the applied voltage and using the same structure. We theoretically investigate the snap-through behavior of the elastic zipping membrane, which can be used to endow the mEMS with voltage-dependent memory, and the theoretical considerations are experimentally validated. As a result, we can apply the mEMS array for robotic memory, such as information writing and erasing; robotic communication by reprogrammable information encrypting, decrypting, and display; robotic computation by electrically reprogrammable logic gates; and reprogrammable binary information transferring. The mEMS represents a comprehensive PI structure for next-generation autonomous machines that can better adapt in unstructured and complex real-world environments.

articles_hidden.title: The ZmJAZ14–ZmMYC2 module regulates anthesis–silking synchrony in maize
articles_hidden.authors: Xiangyu Lu, Di Lv, Shuai Ma, Yu Yan, Chunhui Li, Jiameng Zhu, Liqing Miao, Suzhen Li, Wenzhu Yang, Xiaojin Zhou, Rumei Chen
articles_hidden.abstract: The evolution of traits can increase yield potential but may create physiological constraints. Jasmonic acid (JA) signaling regulates sex determination in male (tassel) and female (ear) inflorescences in maize. Although the formation of ears laid the foundation for high yields, the asynchronous development of the tassel and the ear prolongs the anthesis-silking interval (ASI), threatening reproductive success and reducing yield. Whether JA signaling coordinates ear and tassel development remains unclear. Here, we show that the core JA signaling module, ZmJAZ14-ZmMYC2a/b, orchestrates the expression of SPL29 for reproductive transition, BA1 for female inflorescence initiation, and EXPA5 for silk elongation. Coordination of these physiological processes underpins synchronous growth of the tassel and ears, whereas disruption of ZmMYC2a/b or accumulation of the repressor ZmJAZ14 prolongs ASI. Our work suggests that the repurposing of JA signaling to coordinate ear and tassel development may represent a lineage-specific evolutionary burden in maize. Deciphering the link between gains and unforeseen costs of evolution could further improve yields.

articles_hidden.title: Superoxide dismutase shapes manganese stoichiometry in Southern Ocean diatoms
articles_hidden.authors: J. Scott P. McCain, Loay J. Jabre, Elden Rowland, Jinyoung Jung, Youngju Lee, Tae-Wan Kim, Corina P. D. Brussaard, Rob Middag, Erin M. Bertrand
articles_hidden.abstract: Quantifying the elemental stoichiometry of marine phytoplankton biomass is crucial for projections of primary production. In many cases, the mechanistic underpinnings of biomass stoichiometry are unclear. We combined metaproteomics, Bayesian statistical modeling, and geochemical measurements to quantify the contribution of superoxide dismutases to metal stoichiometry in natural populations of Southern Ocean diatoms. Our analyses indicate that a substantial amount of manganese (Mn) in diatoms in an Antarctic polynya can be attributed to superoxide dismutases (∼0.7 micromoles of Mn:moles of carbon; ∼20% of the total cellular Mn quota). We then used proteomic profiles of polar diatom cultures to identify environmental controls on superoxide dismutases and found that Mn limitation induces the depletion of Mn superoxide dismutases and an accompanying increase in nickel superoxide dismutase. Overall, we combined metaproteomic approaches to quantify proteome composition and connected these measurements to metal-to-carbon ratios and their responses to metal availability. Our approach provides a mechanism for directly parameterizing ecosystem-scale models with molecular measurements.

articles_hidden.title: Structural insights into light harvesting and photosystem II evolution in the basal streptophyte Mesostigma viride
articles_hidden.authors: Tianyu Bai, Zhiyuan Mao, Dapeng Sun, Fei Ma, Bingxin Ma, Yingjie Gao, Yuelin Li, Yi Yang, Wenqiang Tang, Andrew Hitchcock, Matthew P. Johnson, Pu Qian, Yumei Wang, Lirong Tian
articles_hidden.abstract: The basal streptophyte Mesostigma viride represents a critical evolutionary transition toward land plants, yet the molecular basis of its ancestral light-harvesting strategy remains elusive. Here, we present a 2.25-angstrom resolution cryo-EM structure of the M. viride PSII-LHCII-LHCP supercomplex, revealing a unique C 2 S 2 M p2 L p2 -type architecture. Our structure reveals a nearly complete set of conserved PSII core subunits, indicating that much of the PSII structural framework found in terrestrial plants was established early in the streptophyte lineage. At the periphery, the complex features a specialized antenna module in which two ancestral LHCP monomers flank CP29. These ancestral antenna proteins bind an unusually high number of carotenoids, with seven carotenoids per subunit, and extensively incorporate marine-type keto carotenoids, siphonaxanthin, and siphonein, throughout the complex, thereby broadening absorption in the blue-green region. The canonical LHCII trimer exhibits a distinctive chlorophyll b macrocluster and a 96-femtosecond ultrafast energy transfer component. Together, these findings provide a high-resolution molecular framework for an evolutionary intermediate that combines high-capacity aquatic light harvesting with structural features potentially relevant to photoprotection during the transition toward terrestrial life.

articles_hidden.title: Spatial control of enzyme orientation at the lipid droplet interface enables regio- and chemoselective metabolic flux
articles_hidden.authors: So-Hee Son, Sangwon Bae, Soo Young Moon, Minhye Kim, Seung Soo Oh, Chang Yun Son, Ju Young Lee
articles_hidden.abstract: Precise spatial control over multienzyme cascade reactions is increasingly recognized as a design lever in synthetic biology for enhancing catalytic performance and directing metabolic flux. By emulating principles of cellular compartmentalization, synthetic scaffolds and engineered interfaces have emerged as powerful platforms to modulate intermediate channeling and reaction efficiency in complex biocatalytic systems. However, robust and spatially defined immobilization of multienzyme assemblies within physicochemically optimal compartments remains challenging because of the dynamic intracellular environment. Here, we reprogram the amphiphilic interface of yeast lipid droplets (LDs) as a programmable scaffold system to support regio- and chemoselective localization of enzymes. Guided by molecular dynamics simulations, we designed LD-anchoring motifs to direct the enzyme orientation at the LD monolayer interface, yielding cytosol-facing or LD inner-facing configurations. Using this designed LD-anchoring motif, we spatially reorganize a trienzyme cascade for prodeoxyviolacein (PDV) biosynthesis across the cytosol-LD interface, facilitating directional conversion of hydrophilic substrates into hydrophobic products. This spatial reorganization substantially improved PDV production by 1300%, achieving 46.25 milligrams per liter. Our approach offers a modular and tunable platform for engineering spatially organized and readily deployable enzyme cascades, opening avenues for biosynthetic catalysis at organellar interfaces.

articles_hidden.title: Quantum-interference metrology of dissipative Kerr solitons
articles_hidden.authors: Yun-Ru Fan, Yong Geng, Ji Liu, Yong-Jun Huang, Hai-Zhi Song, Hao Li, Li-Xing You, Heng Zhou, Kun Qiu, Kai Guo, Guang-Can Guo, Qiang Zhou
articles_hidden.abstract: Dissipative Kerr solitons in optical microresonators underpin chip-scale frequency combs with applications ranging from coherent telecommunications to precision spectroscopy. Yet the characterization of their intrinsic femtosecond temporal structure remains challenging, as the low pulse energy and broad spectral bandwidth necessitate optical amplification and careful dispersion compensation in conventional ultrafast diagnostics, both of which can substantial distort the waveform. Here, we demonstrate a quantum-interference metrology of microcomb solitons based on Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. By attenuating the soliton stream to the single-photon level and measuring fourth-order interference, we directly retrieve near transform-limited pulse durations without amplification or dispersion management, remaining accurate even after propagation through 25 kilometers of standard fiber. The same interferogram also provides direct access to the temporal separations in multisoliton states by converting intersoliton separations into additional interference dips at corresponding delays, enabling subpicosecond characterization of their intracavity temporal structure. This quantum-inspired paradigm introduces a metrological approach that is immune to amplification and dispersion distortions, offering a powerful tool for the characterization of complex soliton physics.

articles_hidden.title: Temporal dynamics of antigen-specific T cell expansion in primary SARS-CoV-2 infection
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew G. T. Pyo, Adlina Chan, Joshua Rosenheim, Clare Thakker, Lucy Bell, Gayathri Nageswaran, Suzanne Byrne, Ben Killingley, David Scobie, Mariya Kalinova, Alison Boyers, Andrew Catchpole, Alex Mann, Rik G. H. Lindeboom, Marko Z. Nikolic, Sarah A. Teichmann, Helen Wagstaffe, Mahdad Noursadeghi, Christopher Chiu, Curtis G. Callan, Andreas Tiffeau-Mayer, Ned S. Wingreen, Benny Chain
articles_hidden.abstract: Quantifying T cell response during primary infection in humans is crucial for understanding adaptive immunity. Leveraging a controlled human challenge to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, we characterized antigen-specific T cell responses within and across individuals. Notably, individual clones reached similar maximum frequencies despite differences in the timing of their peak expansion. Mathematical modeling within a coarse-grained framework suggested that variability in precursor frequency between different T cell clones could be one mechanism to explain this relationship. Single-cell profiling revealed distinct temporal programs for CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, with CD4 + cells expanding earlier but contracting to a lower frequency. Clones with similar receptors, likely recognizing the same antigen, expanded at similar times. Together, these findings highlight how clone-intrinsic properties such as precursor frequency and CD4/CD8 subset status shape T cell clonal kinetics. These insights provide a quantitative framework for understanding T cell response in humans, with implications for vaccine design.

articles_hidden.title: A robust spin-coupled tetraradical via nonalternant design
articles_hidden.authors: Weixiang Zhou, Yu-Shuang Zhang, Gaetano Ricci, Yubin Fu, David Casanova, Juan Casado, Shang-Da Jiang, Junzhi Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Polyradicals in open-shell polycyclic hydrocarbons (PHs) offer access to multiple spin states and hold great promise for spintronics and quantum technologies. Here we report a nonalternant, air-stable tetraradical featuring two fused 7-5-7 rings and a strongly correlated singlet ground state. This molecule displays an exceptional tetraradical character ( y 0  = 1.00, y 1  = 0.89) and exhibits long ambient stability ( t 1/2  = 33 days). Comprehensive electronic structure and magnetic response analyses reveal that the spin topology is governed by both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions, with robust electron correlation ( J 1  = +321 K, J 2  = −44 K, and J 3  = −29 K). The unique nonalternant design suppresses hyperfine and vibrational decoherence, giving rise to long spin relaxation and coherence time. These findings demonstrate that embedding nonalternant motifs into PH polyradicals provides a powerful strategy to simultaneously promote molecular stability, spin-exchange coupling, and spin robustness—key features for materials in the rising field of quantum information science.

articles_hidden.title: Cell adhesion molecule–related proteins signal to promote cytoneme elongation from Sonic Hedgehog–producing cells
articles_hidden.authors: Christina A. Daly, Miriam E. Dillard, Eric T. Hall, Alfonso Lavado, Jonathon Klein, Jinbin Zhai, Shondra M. Pruett-Miller, Vishwajeeth R. Pagala, Anthony A. High, Alexandre F. Carisey, Christopher C. Hom, Nikki Koehler, Stacey K. Ogden
articles_hidden.abstract: Tissue morphogenesis and postdevelopmental homeostasis rely on efficient information exchange between communicating cells. Cytonemes are actin-based protrusions that contribute to precise information flow by facilitating contact-mediated directional transport of diverse signaling cargoes. How pathway-specific cytonemes are formed is poorly understood, as are the molecular mechanisms promoting actin organization for elongation and stability of the dynamic cellular extensions. We investigated biogenesis of Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) cytonemes, revealing functional repurposing of cell adhesion molecule-related proteins Brother of CDON (BOC) and Cell adhesion molecule-related, Down-regulated by Oncogenes (CDON) into recruiters of actin regulators FARP1 and Cdc42 for cytoneme elongation. Loss of BOC and CDON function blunts protrusion-localized Cdc42 activity, reducing cytoneme lengths and occurrence in SHH-expressing cells. Live imaging of developing murine spinal cords reveals that CDON loss in SHH-expressing cells reduces the frequency of neuroepithelial cytonemes and alters neuronal cell fate specification. These results inform a model whereby SHH-binding proteins promote ligand transport through stimulating formation of long cytonemes.

articles_hidden.title: Dual-action small-molecule VSP-51-2 ameliorates polycystic ovary syndrome via PPARγ modulation and AKR1C3 inhibition
articles_hidden.authors: Xiawen Liu, Xiufen Zheng, Lei Ma, Ziqing Yao, Xuehua Zheng, Miao Liang, Xinhong Wu, Silin Zhang, Xianglin Zhou, Leying Zhu, Zhi Zhou, H. Eric Xu, Wei Yi
articles_hidden.abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), a prevalent multifactorial endocrine disorder, is inadequately managed by current therapies that fail to concurrently target its core metabolic (insulin resistance) and reproductive (hyperandrogenism) pathologies. We report VSP-51-2, a dual-target lead compound initially engineered as a selective PPARγ modulator that unexpectedly exerts potent uncompetitive inhibition of the androgen-synthesizing enzyme AKR1C3 through a putative allosteric mechanism. In preclinical PCOS models, VSP-51-2 restored regular estrous cyclicity, improved ovarian follicular morphology, enhanced systemic insulin sensitivity, suppressed hyperandrogenism, and did not significantly perturb measured hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis hormonal parameters. Mechanistically, it blocks PPARγ phosphorylation at Ser 273 , thereby enhancing adiponectin secretion and GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake, and is predicted to bind a putative allosteric pocket of AKR1C3 to constrain androgen biosynthesis. These findings support VSP-51-2 as a preclinical proof-of-concept compound for a dual-target strategy that addresses metabolic dysfunction and androgen excess through a unified molecular scaffold.

articles_hidden.title: Electron competition in azobenzene programs infection-adaptive antibacterial therapy
articles_hidden.authors: Yongjin Hu, Jiabo Li, Guixian Wang, Xiao Wang, Zhiyuan Zhu, Jingyi Rao
articles_hidden.abstract: Conventional stimulus-responsive antibacterial systems generally operate through binary trigger–activation mechanisms, making them poorly suited to evolving infection microenvironments and thereby contributing to persistent infection and resistance development. Here, we establish an azobenzene-based kinetic regulatory system in which oxygen gradients commonly present in infected tissues continuously program reaction kinetics through electron competition. Oxygen acts as a competing electron acceptor within the reductive reaction network, partitioning electron transfer between azo reduction and oxygen consumption. Substituent electronic structures further reshape reduction propensity, encoding distinct kinetic behaviors. These electronically programmed kinetics translated into adaptive nanoscale dissociation and drug-release profiles: Electron-rich azobenzenes rapidly disassembled under severe hypoxia, whereas electron-withdrawing structures sustained release under mild hypoxia, generating infection state–adaptive antibacterial outputs. Moreover, the same electronic features governing reduction kinetics also reduced the reactivity and toxicity of reductive metabolites. This work establishes electron competition as a strategy for converting environmental gradients into continuous kinetic outputs for adaptive antibacterial therapy.

articles_hidden.title: Comprehensive degron mapping in human transcription factors
articles_hidden.authors: Fia B. Larsen, Vasileios Voutsinos, Nicolas Jonsson, Kristoffer E. Johansson, Freia D. Ethelberg, Isa K. Henrichs, Kresten Lindorff-Larsen, Rasmus Hartmann-Petersen
articles_hidden.abstract: Gene expression is regulated by the targeted degradation of transcription factors through the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Transcription factors destined for degradation are recognized by E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases through motifs termed degrons, embedded within the sequence. In this study, we systematically map degrons in all 1626 human transcription factors. We find thousands of both known and previously unidentified degrons and characterize their sequence properties. Active degrons placed within exposed and intrinsically disordered regions contribute to modulating the abundance of the transcription factors, while the most common somatic mutations that are linked to skin cutaneous melanoma lead to unfolding and exposure of a latent degron buried in the zinc finger structure. We present examples of compartment-specific degrons and demonstrate that variant effects in transcription factors correlate with degron potency. Last, we show that while >60% of all predicted transcriptional activation domains overlap with strong degrons, acidic residues within the remaining transactivating regions counter the degron potency, showing how degrons can shape the transcription factor sequence landscape.

articles_hidden.title: Reciprocal control of genome instability and RNA processing in cancer: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities
articles_hidden.authors: Mariachiara Grieco, Federica Giugliano, Ernesto Guccione, Ilio Vitale, Matteo Cereda
articles_hidden.abstract: Genomic instability and dysregulated RNA processing are each recognized as core hallmarks of cancer, but accumulating evidence indicates that they are mechanistically intertwined rather than independent features. Chromosomal instability, mismatch-repair deficiency, and homologous recombination deficiency can reshape RNA splicing, 3′ end formation, and RNA surveillance through changes in gene dosage, DNA damage signaling, and alterations in regulatory elements. Conversely, aberrant splicing, polyadenylation, and RNA modifications can impair DNA repair, perturb mitotic control, and promote replication stress, thereby reinforcing genomic instability. This bidirectional circuit drives clinically relevant phenotypes, including therapeutic resistance, immune modulation, and emergent vulnerabilities that are not captured by DNA-centric biomarkers alone. Here, we present a unified framework for the genome instability–RNA processing axis and its direct clinical implications for cancer diagnosis, treatment stratification, and therapeutic exploitation, highlighting the most actionable mechanistic interfaces and discussing how integrated DNA-RNA biomarkers and rational combination strategies could extend precision oncology beyond static genomic lesions.

articles_hidden.title: A primordial heavy water reservoir in the outer solar system
articles_hidden.authors: Lindsay P. Keller, Christopher J. Snead, Ming-Chang Liu, Kevin D. McKeegan
articles_hidden.abstract: The oxygen (O) isotopic composition of outer solar system ices is believed to be enriched in heavy O isotopes owing to photochemical processes, but evidence for this O reservoir is exceedingly rare in meteorites. Hydrated interplanetary dust particles (IDPs) collected in Earth’s stratosphere that display high densities of solar energetic particle tracks originate from Edgeworth-Kuiper belt objects. Their mineralogy is dominated by hydrated minerals that formed by alteration of anhydrous precursor minerals at low temperatures through reactions with water (H 2 O)–carbon dioxide fluids. The O isotopic compositions of track-rich hydrated IDPs implicate 17,18 O-rich ices as the source of H 2 O involved in their alteration, providing compelling evidence for the presence of a major heavy water reservoir beyond the orbits of the gas giant planets that was largely isolated from inner solar system materials.

articles_hidden.title: A single–amino acid difference between rodent and human Andes virus affects viral glycoprotein trafficking
articles_hidden.authors: Santiago Vidal-Freire, Natalia M. Ferressini-Gerpe, Carla M. Bellomo, André Filipe Pastor, Maya Tagliavia, Rachel Somavarapu, Shruti Shirsathe, Jayden Zhang, Elaina Giannetti, Ignacio Mena, Florian Krammer, Nicole D. Tischler, Juan Angel Patiño-Galindo, Maria Kaczmarek, Mariano Sanchez-Lockhart, Gabriella Worwa, Jens H. Kuhn, Connie S. Schmaljohn, Adolfo García-Sastre, Valeria P. Martínez, Gustavo Palacios
articles_hidden.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), with rare outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission. A human ANDV isolate from one such outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same region differ in lethality in Syrian golden hamsters. Genomic analysis revealed 25 nonsynonymous substitutions, including one leading to a T641I change in the human ANDV glycoprotein precursor near its cleavage site. Although the isolates differed in growth kinetics, strand-specific RT-qPCR did not support major differences in viral RNA synthesis, whereas virion release was delayed in the case of the human isolate. In human cell expression systems, a single I641T substitution in the human ANDV glycoprotein resulted in decreased Golgi retention and faster release of virion-like particles relative to wild-type glycoprotein. Since ANDV egress takes place at the Golgi, the T641I change present in the human ANDV isolate may represent a human adaptive mutation influencing glycoprotein trafficking and virus particle release.

articles_hidden.title: Reprogramming electron transfer at single-atom Pt sites to break the interference barrier in uric acid detection
articles_hidden.authors: Yifei Chen, Mengxue Zhu, Yinjun Tang, Zhengyi Chen, Jingxin Chang, Ruimin Li, Haifei Wan, Qie Fang, Wenhong Yang, Wenxuan Jiang, Canglong Wang, Liuyong Hu, Wenling Gu, Ming Zhou, Chengzhou Zhu
articles_hidden.abstract: Uric acid (UA) serves as a key biomarker for gout, cardiovascular disease, and kidney dysfunction, yet conventional detection methods relying on H 2 O 2 generation suffer from signal instability and interference from reductive species. Here, we report a uricase-like platinum-nitrogen-carbon nanozyme (Pt-N-C-NH 3 ) that redirects UA oxidation from a two-electron pathway toward a four-electron pathway. By decreasing graphitic nitrogen content, the local electronic microenvironment of platinum sites is modulated, which is associated with a lower calculated free-energy change for the rate-determining absorbed oxygen to absorbed hydroxyl transformation from 1.25 to 0.62 electron volts and thereby promoting oxygen reduction to water. Integrated into a microneedle sensing platform, UA is converted to allantoin for chemiluminescent readout. The sensor exhibits a wide linear range of 50.00 to 1000.00 μM and a detection limit of 15.86 μM, while maintaining 97.57% signal stability against reductive interferents. This work demonstrates that atomic-level coordination engineering enables programmable control over reaction pathways in artificial enzyme systems, thereby facilitating robust biosensing in complex biological environments.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamic plasmonic imaging of electromechanically driven nano-oscillators for charge-resolved multiplex biosensing
articles_hidden.authors: Yunxiao Wang, Xiaoyin Liu, Jingyu Wu, Jinbiao Ma, Baiqi Cui, Guangzhong Ma, Jianxin Ma, Qingjun Liu, Di Wang, Fenni Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Multiplexed profiling of diverse biomarkers is essential for precision diagnostics, but remains challenging for label-free sensors because signals typically scale with analyte mass. Here, we present a dynamic plasmonic imaging platform based on electromechanically driven nano-oscillators for multiplexed, label-free quantification of nucleic acids, proteins, and small molecules within a unified sensing architecture. Size-encoded nanoparticles tethered to a plasmonic surface are electrically actuated to oscillate vertically within the evanescent field and tracked by distance-resolved surface plasmon resonance imaging. Molecular binding alters the effective surface charge of each nano-oscillator, modulating the electrostatic-driven forces and changing oscillation amplitude. This charge-to-motion transduction mechanism reduces dependence on molecular mass and enhances sensitivity for low–molecular weight analytes. This platform simultaneously detects microRNAs, proteins, and small molecules spanning a ∼300-fold molecular weight range within a single field of view. We further demonstrate multiplexed profiling of tumor-associated microRNAs in pretreated supernatants from patient-derived breast cancer cells across 24 clinical samples. Dynamic plasmonic nano-oscillators provide a scalable architecture for multiplex molecular diagnostics.

articles_hidden.title: Humid periods over western Sahara during the Middle Miocene Climate Transition and their implications on the carbon cycle
articles_hidden.authors: Ray Zammit, Caroline H. Lear, Lucas J. Lourens, Paul N. Pearson, Amy Thomas-Sparkes, Marcus P. S. Badger
articles_hidden.abstract: The Middle Miocene expansion of the Antarctic Ice Sheet coincides with major sedimentological changes in Malta. This interval also saw reorganisations in ocean circulation linked to closure of the Mesopotamian Seaway (MSR-events) and perturbations in the carbon cycle (CM events). The final CM event (CM-6), slightly lags the main glacial phase and remains difficult to interpret due to competing mechanisms and conflicting p CO 2 reconstructions. To explore links between cryosphere, circulation, hydroclimate, and the carbon cycle, we present new geochemical records from Malta. Our records show that cryospheric expansion was followed by large, precessionally paced variations in sea-surface salinity and a marked regional increase in biological productivity. The results indicate a shift toward stronger monsoonal influence, delivering enhanced freshwater and nutrient fluxes to the region. This enhanced local biological carbon pump may have acted as a positive feedback to a global CO 2 drawdown. However, any contribution to global CO 2 drawdown remains tentative and cannot be confirmed without contemporaneous high-resolution open-ocean records.

articles_hidden.title: STAT3 controls IL-6–induced epigenomic remodeling and restrains a latent STAT1-associated interferon program in human macrophages
articles_hidden.authors: Yebin Park, Geunho Kwon, Junho Noh, Jaehyun Lee, Keunsoo Kang, Kyung-Hyun Park-Min, Kyuho Kang
articles_hidden.abstract: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a pleiotropic cytokine that drives macrophage functions ranging from tissue homeostasis to inflammation, yet how STAT3 specifies these divergent outcomes remains unclear. By integrating transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with selective STAT3 degradation, we show that STAT3 controls IL-6–induced epigenomic remodeling and restrains a latent STAT1-associated interferon program in human macrophages. Graded STAT3 chromatin recruitment scales with locus-specific H3K27ac deposition and transcriptional output across homeostatic and inflammatory programs. STAT3 degradation permits STAT1 recruitment at a subset of regulatory regions and engages a delayed amplification loop that is partially dependent on STING and type I IFN signaling. In severe COVID-19, monocytes exhibit exaggerated STAT3-associated inflammatory signatures together with attenuated STAT1-associated interferon responses, consistent with a skewed STAT3-STAT1 balance. These findings define a framework in which STAT3 calibrates IL-6–induced chromatin output while maintaining pathway fidelity by limiting STAT1 cross-talk.

articles_hidden.title: Segmented projection image translation for large-area, high-resolution vat photopolymerization
articles_hidden.authors: Jize Dai, Jason M. Kronenfeld, Dan Ilyn, Christopher Linhardt, Philip R. Onffroy, Ian A. Coates, Colin Crown, Michelle Chen, Jacob Dobson, Max A. Saccone, John R. Tumbleston, Maria T. Dulay, Joseph M. DeSimone
articles_hidden.abstract: High-resolution projection-based vat photopolymerization (VP) 3D printing enables rapid fabrication of highly detailed polymeric structures. However, expanding the build area traditionally compromises resolution, creating a fundamental trade-off between projected pixel size and printable area due to fixed digital micromirror device (DMD) pixel counts. Herein, we introduce segmented projection image translation (SPIN), a simple implementation strategy that expands the effective projection area by applying controlled orbital translation to an off-axis objective lens within the optical infinity space. In this work, we demonstrate a projection-based VP printer implemented with SPIN that expands the effective build area by 4.8-fold, from a native field of 60.4 square millimeters to an expanded domain of 290.5 square millimeters. The SPIN-enabled printer produces isolated line features as thin as 9.8 ± 2.2 micrometers and fabricates intricate three-dimensional truss structures with features as small as 30 micrometers. These results validate a practical route for extending microscale projection-based VP printing to larger build areas while preserving feature fidelity across stitched exposure fields.

articles_hidden.title: A full-hardware edge detection system based on a highly robust dual random number generator
articles_hidden.authors: Jikang Xu, Jianlin Wang, Wenjing Liu, Jiaming Zhang, Jingsheng Chen, Xiaobing Yan
articles_hidden.abstract: Conventional edge computing hardware at autonomous driving terminals is limited by chip area and power efficiency for complex image data. Recently, researchers have used memristors to construct dedicated hardware systems, achieving advancements in multiple image processing fields such as pattern recognition and edge detection. However, a full-hardware image processing system with anti-interference, low power, and high real-time performance remains challenging. Here, we fabricated a volatile Ag/AlO x /n-Si memristor with exceptional stability and low power. High-resolution electron microscopy visualized Ag conductive filament formation. Integrating two memristors with a logic circuit, we designed a low-power edge detection unit using dual random number hardware computation. Its energy consumption is 92.3% lower than traditional logic circuits, with strong anti-interference. To validate practical use, we constructed a 32-channel parallel full-hardware system with 64 devices, achieving 31.25 frames per second and excellent edge detection. The system exhibits excellent scalability, stability, and anti-interference, offering great potential for edge vision hardware in autonomous driving, safety monitoring, and surgical assistance.

articles_hidden.title: Incomplete synaptic vesicle priming functionally disconnects CA1 pyramidal cells
articles_hidden.authors: Noemi Holderith, Zoltan Nusser
articles_hidden.abstract: The hippocampal CA1 area is perceived as a nonrecurrent neuronal network, i.e., CA1 pyramidal cells (CA1PCs) within the CA1 area innervate mainly γ-aminobutyric acid–releasing interneurons but not each other. Here, we performed an unbiased examination of the functional properties of local CA1PC output synapses using in vitro two-photon glutamate imaging. Fluorescent transients measured with iGluSnFR3 in individual boutons displayed extraordinary heterogeneity in their amplitudes and short-term plasticity patterns upon a complex train of presynaptic action potential firing. Post hoc electron microscopy of the imaged boutons demonstrated that distinct postsynaptic structure-innervating boutons display different functional properties. Approximately 25% of the boutons innervate CA1PC spines, which either release glutamate with very low release probability or completely fail to release. Phorbol 12,13-dibutyrate and elevated calcium (2+) concentration, manipulations that enhance synaptic vesicle priming and fusion, convert these silent into properly functioning synapses. Our results provide evidence that CA1PCs are interconnected with structurally and molecularly intact glutamatergic synapses, but incomplete synaptic vesicle (SV) priming precludes SV release.

articles_hidden.title: Tracing Neanderthal ancestry patterns through successive population expansions in Europe
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandros Tsoupas, Claudio S. Quilodrán, Jérémy Rio, Mathias Currat
articles_hidden.abstract: During their expansion from Africa, modern humans interbred with Neanderthals, resulting in introgression of Neanderthal DNA into their genomes. This process contributed to a Southeast-to-Northwest gradient of Neanderthal ancestry across Europe. We investigate the population dynamics underlying the emergence and persistence of this gradient through two successive human range expansions. We developed a three-population, layered, spatially explicit simulation framework to track the spatiotemporal evolution of Neanderthal ancestry under a model of interactions among Neanderthals, pre-Neolithic hunter-gatherers, and Neolithic farmers. Our results indicate that the ancestry cline emerged from the interplay between the direction of the initial hunter-gatherer expansion, the northern limit of the Neanderthal range, and strong reproductive isolation, without requiring natural selection. The similar direction of the subsequent Neolithic expansion explains the cline’s persistence and Neanderthal ancestry differences between hunter-gatherers and farmers. These findings demonstrate how spatiotemporal patterns in ancient DNA provide insights into past population dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: Visualizing nanoscopic acoustic mode competition in a van der Waals ferroelectric
articles_hidden.authors: Zhaodong Chu, Carter Fox, Zixin Zhai, Suman Kumari, Haihua Liu, Priti Yadav, Yue Li, Bing Lv, Thomas E. Gage, Jun Xiao, Haidan Wen
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding how low-dimensional ferroelectrics respond to ultrafast excitation at nanoscales is essential for controlling energy flow and mechanical functionality in next-generation polar devices, yet the nanoscopic structural response to ultrafast depolarization remains unresolved, obscuring the microscopic pathways of acoustic decoherence and energy dissipation. Here, we spatiotemporally resolve lattice motion in the van der Waals ferroelectric NbOI 2 using combined ultrafast electron microscopy and diffraction, revealing three acoustic phonons: two transverse shear modes and one longitudinal breathing mode. The transverse mode that shears the layers perpendicular to the in-plane polar axis dominates over that along the polar axis, reflecting anisotropic polarization-strain coupling. Real-space mapping uncovers spatially correlated heterogeneity in mode amplitudes and lifetimes. Regions dominated by a single shear mode exhibit significantly longer acoustic lifetimes than multimode regions, suggesting acoustic phonon–phonon scattering as a major source of decoherence. Our results provide a microscopic understanding of ultrafast depolarization-driven acoustic dynamics and spatially heterogeneous energy dissipation in van der Waals ferroelectrics.

articles_hidden.title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica
articles_hidden.authors: Layla A. Schuster, Beibei Liu, Jose Cleydson F. Silva, Xi Cheng, Raquel Dias, Meixia Zhao
articles_hidden.abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.

articles_hidden.title: Dual-acting compounds that deliver an acidifying domain via zanamivir to the virus surface are potent influenza inhibitors
articles_hidden.authors: Charley Mackenzie-Kludas, Wen-Yang Wu, Betty Jin, Jennifer L. McKimm-Breschkin, Ee Ling Seah, Paul Jones, Emily Fairmaid, Celeste M. K. Tai, Ding Yuan Oh, Peter J. Jenkins, Aeron C. Hurt, Lorena E. Brown
articles_hidden.abstract: While contemporary antiviral development primarily strives to produce “lock and key” inhibitors, we present here a different approach to drug design that uses compounds devised to alter the microenvironment of the virion surface, making it incompatible with virus entry. We illustrate this strategy with inhibitors of influenza virus and show that compounds designed to produce a proton-rich mantle above the virion surface affect the ability of the viral hemagglutinin to interact with cellular receptors and gain entry to the cell. The compounds show exceptional antiviral activity both in vitro and in vivo and protect against influenza illness in ferrets and in mice after a single dose, either therapeutically or prophylactically.

articles_hidden.title: Photonic entanglement swapping with remote quantum dots
articles_hidden.authors: Mattia Beccaceci, Giuseppe Ronco, Fabrizio Cienzo, Pierpaolo Bassetti, Alessandro Laneve, Francesco Basso Basset, Tobias M. Krieger, Thomas Oberleitner, Quirin Buchinger, Francesco Salusti, Barbara Souza Damasceno, Silke Kuhn, Saimon F. Covre da Silva, Sandra Stroj, Klaus D. Jöns, Sven Höfling, Tobias Huber-Loyola, Armando Rastelli, Michele B. Rota, Rinaldo Trotta
articles_hidden.abstract: Entanglement swapping is a protocol that details how to create entanglement between previously uncorrelated particles. Its photonic version, mediated by the interference of photon pairs generated by separate quantum systems, finds disparate applications in quantum networks. So far, entanglement swapping with entangled photons from remote systems has been implemented only using probabilistic sources. However, the scaling up of quantum networks requires nonprobabilistic quantum emitters without a trade-off between the degree of entanglement and photon-pair generation rate. Here, we demonstrate photonic entanglement swapping using photon pairs generated by two separate GaAs quantum dots. The emitters are deterministically embedded in hybrid semiconductor-piezoelectric devices that make the entangled photons from two dissimilar quantum dots nearly identical. Entanglement swapping is demonstrated with a fidelity as high as 0.71(2), more than 10 SDs above the classical limit. The experimental data are quantitatively explained by a theoretical model that also suggests how to boost the protocol performance. Our work opens the path to the exploitation of quantum dot entangled-photon sources in quantum repeater networks.

articles_hidden.title: Nonlinear cooling and control of a mechanical quantum harmonic oscillator
articles_hidden.authors: Matteo Simoni, Ivan Rojkov, Matteo Mazzanti, Wojciech Adamczyk, Alexander Ferk, Pavel Hrmo, Shreyans Jain, Tobias Sägesser, Daniel Kienzler, Jonathan Home
articles_hidden.abstract: Nonlinearities are a key feature allowing nonclassical control of quantum harmonic oscillators. However, when nonlinearities are strong, designing protocols for control is often difficult, placing a barrier to exploiting these properties fully. In this work, using a single trapped-ion oscillator operated in the strongly nonlinear regime of the atom-light interaction, we show how to generate localized multi (two, three, four, and five)–component Schrödinger’s cat manifolds using a novel form of nonlinear reservoir engineering. We then specifically select Hamiltonians which allow us to perform measurements on these state manifolds. Our work demonstrates the experimental use of high-order nonlinear processes for control of nonclassical states of a quantum harmonic oscillator, opening up a new toolbox which can be applied to bosonic quantum error correction, computation, and sensing.

articles_hidden.title: CD8 + T cells induce RIPK1-regulated brain endothelial cell death in cerebral malaria
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandros Hadjilaou, Phaidon Christodoulou, Johannes Brandi, Jan Broder Engler, Ana Matcharashvili, Tatiana Goncharov, Carla Johnson, Nikita Vladimirov, Charlotte Schubert, Sanjib Mohanty, Praveen K. Sahu, Linda Drewicke, Sonja Binder, Oliver Kretz, Susanne Krasemann, Lukas C. Bal, Marcel S. Woo, Sandra Konrath, Dagmara McGuinness, Vanessa Vieira, Ulricke Richardt, Christiane Steeg, Simone Bauer, Terrie Taylor, James Nyirenda, Thomas Renné, Karl B. Seydel, Angelika Hoffmann, Jens Kuhle, Zhen Huang, Peter Vandenabeele, Andrew Woehler, Christopher A. Moxon, Markus Schwaninger, Samuel C. Wassmer, Victor G. Puelles, Domagoj Vucic, Thomas Jacobs, Manuel A. Friese
articles_hidden.abstract: Cerebral malaria (CM) is a potentially lethal complication of Plasmodium falciparum infection characterized by blood-brain barrier disruption and brain hemorrhage. Although immune-mediated endothelial damage is central to CM pathology, the mechanisms linking cytotoxic immune responses to endothelial injury remain unclear. Here, we show that CD8 + T cells induce receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)–regulated cell death of brain endothelial cells in mouse CM, while RIPK1 phosphorylation is increased in brain endothelial cells in human CM. Using magnetic resonance imaging, three-dimensional tissue-cleared brain imaging, cross-species pathology, endothelial translatomics, immunocerebrovascular interactomics, and genetic association testing, we identify a CD8 + T cell–dependent, RIPK1-centered mouse endothelial cell death program. Combined RIPK1 and caspase inhibition protected cross-presenting endothelial cells from CD8 + T cell–mediated death in vitro. In vivo, brain endothelial-specific genetic inactivation or systemic pharmacological inhibition of RIPK1 kinase activity prolonged survival in mouse CM without altering parasitemia. These findings support RIPK1 inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy to counter CD8 + T cell–induced endothelial death in CM.

articles_hidden.title: Weak adsorption, strong consequences: How trace gases control ice growth and quasi-liquid-layer structure
articles_hidden.authors: Cooper J. Yerby, Xiangyu Chen, Gabriel Gonsalves Bertho, Chongqing Zhu, Joseph S. Francisco, Dai-Bei Yang
articles_hidden.abstract: Gases in the atmosphere are often treated as passive background species in cold environments, yet their molecular roles at icy interfaces remain poorly understood. Here, we show how hydrophobic and hydrophilic trace gases can actively reorganize the ice interface and regulate freezing through interfacial stabilization. We find these gases can actively modulate both the kinetics and thermodynamics of the water-ice interface. Using molecular simulations, we find that all gases examined retard ice-front propagation relative to pure water to different extents. This slowing arises from weak but preferential adsorption at the water-ice interface, where gases occupy water-dense interfacial layers and locally suppress ice-like ordering. After freezing is complete, gases do not distribute uniformly across the frozen surface, but partition selectively among multiple adsorption regions across the ice–quasi-liquid-layer (QLL)–air interfacial landscape. Relatively hydrophobic gases exhibit a three-region adsorption pattern, whereas relatively hydrophilic gases occupy only two dominant adsorption regions. Despite these differences, both classes preferentially accumulate near the QLL-air boundary and its immediate outer region rather than the ice-QLL interface. There, gases pair with and compensate for dangling surface bonds (through a surface-passivating effect reminiscent of ligand stabilization), reducing the thermodynamic driving force for premelting and thereby thinning the QLL. These results establish a unified molecular picture in which atmospheric gases are active interfacial modulators of both ice growth and ice structure, with implications for freezing, ice-cloud microphysics, and heterogeneous atmospheric chemistry.

articles_hidden.title: Inhibition of aberrant astrocyte activity restores auditory sensorimotor function in zebrafish spen mutants
articles_hidden.authors: Yan Gao, Anna Shipman, Peng Sun, Na Zhang, Eliot T. Smith, Itallia Pacentine, Alex Nechiporuk, Teresa Nicolson
articles_hidden.abstract: Sensorimotor deficits can profoundly affect the life quality of patients with neurological disorders, yet our understanding of central dysfunction at the cellular or circuit level is limited. Using a forward genetic approach to generate loss of auditory function in zebrafish larvae, we identified a recessive mutation in split ends ( spen ), which encodes a transcription factor implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders in humans. We found that auditory sensorimotor deficits in spen mutants are associated with chronically elevated calcium levels in hindbrain radial astrocytes. Astrocytes have been previously implicated in the integration of neuronal inputs that alter arousal states and sensorimotor behavior. Inhibition of noradrenergic receptors, which are expressed in astrocytes, lowered calcium levels in mutant radial astrocytes and, notably, restored behavioral responses to sound in spen mutants. Our study highlights a role for noradrenergic signaling in spen -related disease and points to potential therapeutic approaches for pediatric patients.

articles_hidden.title: A transcriptional and cellular exploration of obesity and type II diabetes in human adipose tissues
articles_hidden.authors: William V. Trim, Kseniia Petrova, Katie Healy, Brenneth M. Stevens, John G. Scanlan, Heather J. Faust, Sara Svensson Akusjärvi, Katie L. O’Brien, Donal O’Shea, Michael B. Brenner, Helen Heneghan, Lydia Lynch
articles_hidden.abstract: Obesity is tightly linked to metabolic disorders such as type II diabetes mellitus (T2D), although a subpopulation of individuals with obesity do not present with these morbidities. The biological factors conferring T2D vulnerability remain incompletely understood. We recruited 58 individuals with obesity with or without a clinical diagnosis of T2D (Ob + T2D and Ob). We profiled paired samples of omental and subcutaneous adipose by single-cell RNA sequencing ( n  = 10), flow cytometry under basal and stimulated conditions ( n  = 42), and histology ( n  = 17). Flow cytometry and chemokine quantification were also performed in paired whole blood. We identified reprogramming of the omental stromal compartment, centered on mesothelial and endothelial cells, alongside contrasting innate T cell and macrophage phenotypes across depots. Mesothelial and IGFBP2 + cells exhibited a fibrotic, epithelial-mesenchymal transition–like phenotype, while omental endothelial cells exhibited a lipid-overload, inflammatory, antigen presentation profile in T2D. Omental and subcutaneous adipose innate T cells exhibited divergent inflammatory profiles between tissues. These findings reveal previously unidentified insights into the pathophysiology of T2D in adipose tissue and identify compensatory networks within the tissues that could be exploited by targeted therapeutics.

articles_hidden.title: High-impulse and reactant-regenerative combustion-based micro actuators
articles_hidden.authors: Jihong Yin, Dongkai Wang, Dazhe Zhao, Yanting Gong, Junwen Zhong
articles_hidden.abstract: The use of combustibles in micro-actuator technologies enables powerful impulsive actuation capabilities comparable to those of natural organisms. However, the exogenous dependence of fuel limits the development of combustion-based actuators. We present a closed-cycle reactant regeneration strategy wherein the bidirectional interconversion between hydrogen and water achieves real-time fuel replenishment for reactant-regenerative electrolysis and combustion reactions. Based on this, we develop a 1.5-centimeter actuator that generates forces above 20 newtons and operates continuously for >7200 cycles without refueling (a two orders-of-magnitude improvement over existing combustion-based actuators). Experiments confirm its strength and cross-environment versatility for removing obstacles, jetting, and striking via underwater cavitation. These features enable the actuator to be integrated into small robotic platforms, allowing them to reconfigure local surroundings in an active manner.

articles_hidden.title: Structure of the Chimalliviridae bacteriophage Goslar reveals host recognition and infection machinery
articles_hidden.authors: Dwaipayan Basu, Yajie Gu, Ying-Xing Li, Taylor Forman, Majid Ghassemian, Ryan K. Min, Joe Pogliano, Kevin D. Corbett
articles_hidden.abstract: Large-genome bacteriophages (phages) of the Chimalliviridae family have a distinctive life cycle, building compartments inside infected bacterial cells that broadly protect their genomes from host defenses. Here, we use cryo–electron microscopy to determine a structure of the Escherichia coli –infecting Chimalliviridae phage Goslar. We combine manual modeling of 25 structural proteins with AlphaFold structure predictions of an additional three proteins to generate a composite model with 2888 protein chains from 28 different structural proteins, totaling more than 1.4 million amino acid residues. Our structure reveals the architecture of the Goslar capsid, portal, tail, and baseplate, highlighting structural similarities and differences with other tailed phages. Combining our structural data with quantitative mass spectrometry of Goslar virions, we identify several high-copy virion-associated proteins that likely play key roles when injected into host cells upon infection. We also identify a Chimalliviridae -specific family of proteins that form long, flexible filaments anchored at the phage baseplate and which incorporate carbohydrate-binding domains, suggesting a key role in host recognition.

articles_hidden.title: Prebiotic magnetite enables chirality-magnetic surface feedback
articles_hidden.authors: José A. P. M. Devienne, Ziwei Liu, Clancy Zhijian Jiang, Nicholas J. Tosca, Thomas Ginnis, Dimitar D. Sasselov, Richard J. Harrison, S. Furkan Ozturk
articles_hidden.abstract: The emergence of biomolecular homochirality requires both an initial symmetry-breaking event and a mechanism to amplify and preserve a chiral imbalance. Magnetic minerals have been shown to function as chiral agents through the chiral-induced spin selectivity (CISS) effect and may have enabled homochirality on early Earth, yet the magnetic properties of magnetite formed under realistic prebiotic conditions remain unexplored. Here, we show that magnetite synthesized through two geochemically plausible pathways—UV-driven photo-oxidation and nitrite-mediated oxidation of Fe(II)—produces particles dominated by single-vortex and multivortex magnetic domain states. Magnetic measurements and electron microscopy confirm that these populations differ markedly from the nano-fabricated thin-film substrates conventionally used in previous CISS experiments. Using three-dimensional micromagnetic simulations, we demonstrate that single-domain and vortex-state grains undergo irreversible, exchange-driven remagnetization when interacting with spin-polarized homochiral compounds. This magnetic irreversibility provides a robust mechanism for storing and reinforcing weak chiral bias, suggesting that prebiotic magnetite could have contributed to the emergence and stabilization of persistent chiral bias on early Earth.

articles_hidden.title: Real-time complex-valued RF blind source separation via in-physics computing
articles_hidden.authors: Jiajia Wang, Shuran Zhang, Haoran Zhang, Yifu Xu, Shifan Chen, Peiming Yan, Zhihui Liu, Xiaotian Zhu, Shuying Li, Yuyang Liu, Sha Zhu, Chao Wang, Yunping Bai, Chaoran Huang, Sai T. Chu, David J. Moss, Xingyuan Xu, Kun Xu
articles_hidden.abstract: The rise of edge-centric 6G networks demands real-time intelligent processing of heterogeneous radio-frequency (RF) signals. Complex-valued blind source separation (CV-BSS) provides a physical-layer capability, enabling the blind extraction of source components from overlapping RF signals. Here, we demonstrate an integrated photonic vector processor (IPVP) that implements real-time CV-BSS via in-physics computation directly on raw RF signals. The IPVP operates across multiple RF bands up to 24 GHz and achieves blind, in-hardware adaptation to unknown sources and channels via in situ learning. Experiments demonstrate the efficacy of IPVP in multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communications and multi-band radar interference suppression. The IPVP reduces the EVMs of the two recovered signals from over 50% to 6.18% and 5.3%, respectively, while enhancing the SIR by up to 26 dB. This work demonstrates, to our knowledge, the first photonic processor capable of real-time CV-BSS at RF, highlighting the potential of integrated photonic hardware for ultralow-latency, edge-intelligent signal processing.

articles_hidden.title: Ultrafast Meissner-levitated microrotor
articles_hidden.authors: Joel K. Jose, Andrea Marchese, Marion Cromb, Hendrik Ulbricht, Andrejs Cebers, Ping Koy Lam, Tao Wang, Andrea Vinante
articles_hidden.abstract: Levitated mechanical systems offer a powerful and flexible platform for the realization of ultralow-noise sensors and tests of fundamental physics. Here, we report the demonstration of a levitated microrotor, consisting of a magnetic microsphere levitated by the Meissner effect at 4.2 kelvin. The rotor reaches rotation frequencies above 2.3 megahertz (138 million revolutions per minute) while exhibiting an exceptionally low damping rate of 4.75 × 10 −7  hertz. Exploiting the linear dependence of friction on the gas density, we demonstrate high-accuracy absolute pressure sensing over a wide range at cryogenic temperature. Last, we detect the thermal torque noise at intermediate pressure by operating the rotor in synchronized mode, resulting in a first preliminary narrowband search for axion-like dark matter. More broadly, the combination of high rotational speed, low temperature, and low thermal torque noise establishes a previously unidentified regime for precision measurements, with direct implications for the detection of extremely weak forces and fields.

articles_hidden.title: Phototropin-mediated blue light signaling orients the asymmetry of Marchantia polymorpha spores
articles_hidden.authors: Johannes Roetzer, Radka Slovak, Eva-Sophie Wallner, Natalie Edelbacher, Beate Asper, Sebastian Deiber, Sebastian Seitner, Martin Colombini, Liam Dolan
articles_hidden.abstract: Multicellular organisms produced by sexual reproduction develop from single cells, and the asymmetry of these cells can define the orientation of the earliest developmental axes. The haploid multicellular stage of the plant, Marchantia polymorpha, develops from a single cell—the spore—that divides asymmetrically, producing an apical germ cell that generates the plant body and a smaller basal cell that differentiates as an anchoring germ rhizoid cell. We show that the orientation of this asymmetric cell division is controlled by an external environmental cue—blue light—that is perceived by the photoreceptor phototropin. This process requires the NCH1 (NRL PROTEIN FOR CHLOROPLAST MOVEMENT 1) protein for downstream signaling. Together, these findings define core elements of the mechanism by which a directional environmental signal orients cell division, which, in turn, orients the first axis of symmetry.

articles_hidden.title: Single-cell profiling of the duodenum during chronic human norovirus infection
articles_hidden.authors: Yuki Matsushima, Jessica Durkee-Shock, Derron A. Alves, Bianca M. Nagata, Sun A. Kim, Eunice C. Chan, Natthawan Chaimongkol, Ryoka Ishiyama, Karenna Barton, Alison Han, Libby A. Kelly, Princess U. Ogbogu, Sheila Kumar, Xixi Xu, Kristi C. Briggs, Kosuke Murakami, Jeffrey I. Cohen, Michael D. Keller, Stanislav V. Sosnovtsev, Kim Y. Green
articles_hidden.abstract: Human noroviruses are a major cause of diarrheal disease, yet their pathogenesis remains poorly defined. We performed single-cell RNA sequencing of duodenal biopsies and matched stem cell–derived enteroids from immunodeficient individuals with chronic norovirus infection. Norovirus RNA was detected primarily in enterocytes, enteroendocrine cells, and macrophages, with the highest proportion of viral RNA-positive cells observed among M2 macrophages, followed by late enterocytes. Despite this distribution, late enterocytes produced higher viral yields than differentiated M2 macrophages in vitro. Norovirus infection was associated with the up-regulation of MHC class I-related genes and IL15 in duodenal macrophages and late enterocytes, together with increased IFNG expression by CD8 T cells. Macrophages and late enterocytes up-regulated CXCL9 and CXCL10/11 , respectively, consistent with CD8 and CD4 T cell recruitment to the duodenum. These findings show that noroviruses infect and persist across multiple permissive cell types during chronic infection, resulting in marked dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses that may drive pathogenesis.

articles_hidden.title: MYC primes a paralog synthetic lethality involving the mitochondrial translocase subunits TIMM17A and TIMM17B and N-Acetylaspartate
articles_hidden.authors: Sydney M. Moyer, Nina Ilic, Sydney Gang, Lucas Dailey, Sehyun Oh, Jasmine Stavridi, Gaia Taig, Kathia E. Rodarte, Joseph D. DeAngelo, Andrea Jiang, Brian H. Shim, Jonathan P. Rennhack, John R. Jacob, Melis A. Akinci, Jonathan So, Helen Wang, Federica Piccioni, Jessica A. Talamas, Hans R. Widlund, David E. Root, Clary B. Clish, Nika N. Danial, William C. Hahn
articles_hidden.abstract: To identify the genes and pathways required for the survival of MYC -amplified cancers, we engineered an isogenic cell system in which transformation is driven by oncogenic MYC . Using a genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 library, we identified the mitochondrial membrane translocase TIMM17A as uniquely essential for the survival of MYC-transformed cells. This dependency arises from MYC-driven suppression of TIMM17B , the paralog of TIMM17A . TIMM17A/B is an essential component of the TIM23 mitochondrial protein import complex, and the MYC-induced suppression of TIMM17B creates a strong dependency on TIMM17A . N-acetylaspartate supplementation rescued TIMM17A dependency in MYC -amplified cell lines, highlighting the unique and crucial role of this metabolite in the cell fitness of MYC -amplified cancers. These observations identify a paralog dependency required for the survival of a subset of MYC-driven cancers.

articles_hidden.title: The (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide is a microbe-derived NAD + precursor that drives gut stem cell renewal
articles_hidden.authors: Jiangmeng Han, Jayson M. Antonio, Jagannatham Naidu Bhupana, Garam Choi, Jiaxing Yang, Eric Chiles, Yan Tong, Mohamed Asik Rajmohamed, Hung-Ting Wu, Dahui Wang, Vik Meadows, Nicolas Lapaque, Jean-Pierre Etchegaray, Rafal Filip, Ta-Chiang Liu, Pawel R. Kiela, Nicholas Bessman, Ronaldo P. Ferraris, Ching-On Wong, Xiaoyang Su, Nan Gao
articles_hidden.abstract: Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD) is a critical cellular coenzyme whose decline associates with various chronic and inflammatory diseases. Improved NAD restoration may reduce disease risks and extend healthy lifespan. We report here that certain commensal bacteria including specific probiotic species produce (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide (N-MNA), which is a structural isomer of methylnicotinamide, a nicotinamide degradative metabolite. Patients with gut dysbiosis and inflammation show reduced stool N-MNA. Stable isotope tracing revealed that N-MNA can be rapidly taken up and incorporated into NAD redox reactions by intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) and non-IECs of fruit fly, mouse, and human. Genetic and pharmacological analyses suggest that N-MNA is converted to NAD + via the Preiss-Handler pathway, independent of the salvage pathway. Cell-type-specific ablation or overexpression of SIRT1, an NAD-consuming enzyme, in Drosophila , along with intestinal stem cell (ISC) lineage tracing in mice revealed that systemic N-MNA supplementation promotes ISC regeneration and gut epithelial repair. Compared to known NAD precursors, N-MNA brings a methyl group into host cells, representing a class of microbe-derived NAD precursor that stimulates the tissue regenerative power.

articles_hidden.title: Arbitrarily cuttable and ultrathin MXene structural colors for customizable and wearable multispectral information management
articles_hidden.authors: Chunxiao Wu, Huhu Cheng, Chuanxin Weng, Chen Luo, Qihua Liao, Kaixuan Zhu, Yajie Hu, Leilei Liang, Bin Wang, Yan Li, Liangti Qu
articles_hidden.abstract: Structural colors based on natural and artificial microstructures show promising light manipulation. As atomically thick building blocks, Ti 3 C 2 T x sheets have been successfully assembled into the ultrathin, flexible, arbitrarily cuttable, large-size structural colors by the simple and low-cost spray methods based on the lossy thin-film interference. By ordered stacking atomically thick Ti 3 C 2 T x layer by layer at well-organized low–surface tension semidry assemble state, rich colors from yellow to gray with the thickness from ∼22 to ∼154 nanometers of uniform Ti 3 C 2 T x colors are obtained, having the thinnest framework among solution-processed flexible structural colors with similar optical performance. Low-infrared emissivity from room to 300°C temperature and region-selective patterns make highly information-fused and complex visible-infrared (VIS-IR) Ti 3 C 2 T x colors camouflage. Without conventional dielectric layer between Ti 3 C 2 T x and substrate, automated spraying system can produce meter-scale films that can be cut and sewn into VIS-IR concealment “camouflage cloaks” easily, promising ultrathin multifunctional information systems and beyond.

articles_hidden.title: Basin-scale changes in net primary production from the biogeochemical-Argo array
articles_hidden.authors: Thomas J. Ryan-Keogh, Sandy J. Thomalla
articles_hidden.abstract: Marine net primary production is expected to be affected by climate change. Although remote sensing offers broad spatial and temporal coverage, it is limited to surface observations and cannot capture subsurface variability. Autonomous profiling floats provide critical depth-resolved measurements that help bridge this gap. Here, we use data from the biogeochemical-Argo array to estimate basin-scale change in net primary production using the carbon-based production algorithm. We find statistically significant negative trends across the Atlantic and Southern Oceans and positive trends in the Pacific Ocean. These changes, if occurring in response to climate forcing, raise concern due to the key role of phytoplankton productivity in sustaining marine ecosystems. These trends typically agree in direction and magnitude with those from satellites. Our findings highlight the value of the biogeochemical-Argo array in detecting change in ocean productivity, demonstrating its potential for sustained monitoring. These results underscore the need for integrated observing systems to capture the full extent of changing marine productivity.

articles_hidden.title: Strigolactone receptor D14 integrates phosphate and strigolactone signaling by interacting with and stabilizing PHR1
articles_hidden.authors: Haiyang Yu, Meng Zhang, Yihang Zhang, Jindong Li, Liu Yang, Yuehua Wang, Li Chen, Ruifeng Yao
articles_hidden.abstract: Strigolactone (SL) and low phosphate (LP) signaling coordinately regulate shoot and root architecture and plant adaptation. While LP signaling is generally considered upstream of SL biosynthesis, their interaction is more complex. For instance, exogenous SL exerts opposite effects on lateral root formation under low versus high phosphorus. Here, we show that under LP, SL-induced anthocyanin accumulation requires PHR1, demonstrating that PHR1 functions downstream of SL signaling. We uncovered an SL-dependent physical interaction between PHR1 and the SL receptor DWARF14 (D14). This interaction promotes PHR1 dimerization, stabilizes PHR1 by inhibiting its ubiquitination-mediated degradation, and enhances its transcriptional activation activity. The D14-PHR1 complex directly binds and up-regulates the SL biosynthesis gene MAX3 and anthocyanin biosynthesis genes, thereby inhibiting branching and hypocotyl elongation and promoting anthocyanin accumulation. These findings indicate that PHR1 mediates the coordination of SL and LP signaling, potentially explaining SL’s opposing effects on lateral root formation under different phosphorus conditions. In the phr1 mutant, exogenous SL inhibited lateral roots under both LP and Pi-sufficient conditions, confirming that the promoting role of SL under LP requires PHR1. PHR1 also interacted with D14 to activate LBDs and HB23 , regulating lateral root formation. Collectively, LP signaling coordinates with SL signaling via two parallel pathways: regulating SL biosynthesis to align SL functions with LP requirements and enhancing PHR1 activity through PHR1-D14 interaction to amplify LP signaling outputs.

articles_hidden.title: Mevalonate pathway regulates double-negative regulatory T cell stability in metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease
articles_hidden.authors: Hua Jin, Xiyu Wang, Longyang Zhou, Xinjie Zhong, Yunxiong Wei, Xiaotong Han, Nan Xu, Peiyang Fang, Zihan Zhang, Xiaonan Du, Mengyi Li, Songlin Wang, Zhongtao Zhang, Guangyong Sun, Dong Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Lipid metabolism dysfunction and immune imbalance are critical pathogenic drivers of metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).
